speechtext: I have the honour to inform the House that I have received a communication notifying me that a vacancy has occurred in the representation, namely, Jean Chretien, Esq., Member for the electoral district of Saint-Maurice, by resignation. Accordingly I have addressed my warrant to the Chief Electoral Officer for the issue of a new writ of election for the said electoral district.

speakeroldname: Right Hon. John N. Turner (Leader of the Opposition):
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I appreciate you allowing me the opportunity to say a few words. This morning at five after ten Mr. Chretien arrived in my office with a letter of resignation as the Member of Parliament for Saint-Maurice and told me that he was going to see you immediately thereafter. I said to the Hon. Member that it was a shock, that the country needed him, that certainly the Liberal Party needed him, and that I did as well in personal terms. I asked him if there was any way we could reopen the question and try to resolve matters to his satisfaction. He said that after 23 years as a Member of Parliament he felt he had made his contribution to this House and to the country, and that now he wanted to place his family first and seek other opportunities.
It became clear that despite my attempt to persuade him differently his course of action had been set, Your Honour. I understand he did see you and presented his resignation to the House.

1 must say that Jean Chretien is a great Canadian, who served his country for twenty-three years as a Member of this House, and who served his constituents in the district of Saint-Maurice, with distinction, tremendous flair and limitless dedication. In the course of his career he has held some very important positions. It would take too long to summarize Jean Chretien's entire career, but two events stand out, and especially his efforts during the Quebec Referendum. Under the leadership of Mr. Trudeau, Jean Chretien marshalled the forces of the federal wing of the party to work together with Mr. Ryan and others, and to represent and lead the federalist forces in Quebec, and he did so very successfully. This country
and the province of Quebec will never forget Jean Chretien's efforts in this respect.
During the negotiations for patriating our Constitution and enshrining the Charter of Rights and Freedom in that Constitution, Jean Chretien, as Minister of Justice, played a key role. So there was the Referendum, our Constitution, the first Francophone to be appointed by the then Prime Minister to the position of Minister of Finance, and a superb Minister of Indian Affairs and Northern Development who was very proud of the fact he had inaugurated more national parks than any other minister: all this adds up to an unparallelled career and a unique Member of this House. We will miss Jean Chretien in the House of Commons, and I am sure that my opinion is shared by all.
I wish Mr. Chretien and his family, as I have already said privately, the very best. He deserves the gratitude of all his fellow Canadians, and I hope that Jean Chretien, his wife Aline, and the whole family-he became a grandfather for the third time yesterday-I wish him the best of luck. His name, presence and personality will never be forgotten in this House.

Mr. Speaker, I want to congratulate my hon. friend, the Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner) on the warmth and sincerity with which he spoke of a great Quebecer and a great Canadian. Jean Chretien has resigned. He was a brave and dedicated Member who served Canadians and his constituents with energy and dignity. This extremely likeable man has made an unforgettable impression on all Canadians.
As a Quebecer, 1 remember more specifically his steadfast and courageous leadership during the Referendum campaign, since I worked for him at the time. He showed great leadership and generosity towards all his collaborators, and he showed understanding for the position of his opponents.

He was-I should not speak of Jean in the past tense-he is gone, but only from this House. As a Member of Parliament and a colleague, he was witty and compassionate. He was partisan and caring. He loves Quebec and believes very deeply in Canada and has a unique and thoughtful way of expressing that.
1 still have some of the scars to prove his effectiveness. There were moments in Central Nova when I doubted whether I would ever see this House. Jean Chretien would arrive in New Glasgow, Pictou or Stellarton and create, as he did, a very favourable impression, which dismayed me at the time

February 27, 1986
Resignation-Mr. Chretien
but which I salute today. So we in the House say goodbye to Jean Chretien and his wife and family with our affectionate good wishes.

Mr. Speaker, I want to join with the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) and the Right Hon. Leader of the Official Opposition (Mr. Turner) in expressing my regret and, I must say, surprise, at Jean Chretien's decision to leave the House of Commons to embark on whatever career he has decided upon. I do not believe there is anyone in the country who would deny that in the 23 years he has been here he has served with dynamism, honesty and courage. He stood up for everything he believed in all of the time.
One never had to doubt where one stood with Jean Chretien. He made it quite clear when he agreed with you that he agreed with you vigorously, and when he opposed you that he opposed you vigorously. He has left a lasting impression on all Hon. Members of the House of Commons who were here during his 23 years.
He seems to me to be a man who will always place the people of Canada first in his efforts, both on behalf of Canadian federalism and on behalf of Canadian independence. He left a mark not only with those of us who were here to watch him, alongside others, fight the battle, but he also left us a legacy and I believe the majority of Canadians would agree that they owe him a debt of gratitude.
He was always available to new Members of Parliament. When I first came to the House of Commons Jean Chretien was on the Government side. He was the first one who came to welcome me to the House of Commons. It was Jean Chretien who invited me, as a newly elected Member of Parliament, using himself as an example, to attempt to learn some of the other official language in order that I could play a more meaningful role. I am personally grateful to him for that kind of understanding. He has a sense of humour which allows for an easing of tensions when tensions grow up. He was always able to find a funny way of putting something which ensured there would not be a lasting breach develop between Hon. Members when they had disagreements.
I hope that Jean Chretien's departure from politics is a temporary departure. I hope he will at some point return to politics in one way or another and will continue to serve the public of Canada.
I have received notice that there are two Hon. Members who want to make comments. I will allow them both to do so briefly and then we will go on to Routine Proceedings.

Mr. Speaker, as Chairman of the Quebec Caucus and an old friend of Jean Chretien, I would like to pay tribute to his tireless dedication to the work he did in this House.
As a person, a Member, and a Liberal, Jean Chretien has always seen Canadian unity as one of his greatest concerns,
but he was also a Francophone Quebecer, a French Canadian who wanted to project and demonstrate his pride in that fact, and often, when talking to his Quebec colleagues and the people of Quebec generally, he gave himself as an example of a unilingual Francophone who managed to make his mark at the national level and at the same time served the interests of his constituency and his province, and served them well.
On behalf of my colleagues, and especially the Liberal Members from Quebec, I want to thank him for what he did, and I also wish to thank him on behalf of all Canadians. I wish him the best of luck in his new career in the private sector, and I want to remind him that... well, Jean Chretien and I started together in politics in the fifties at the Laval University Liberal Club. So we have many memories of battles against Maurice Duplessis and subsequent election campaigns.
I realize that his decision was not an easy one, since at one time I myself had to make that decision. I know it is not easy, and I want to thank him for everything he has done for Quebec and for Canada and wish him the best of luck in his new career.

Mr. Speaker, I want to take this opportunity to say that I am losing a personal friend, and 1 want that to be clear. He has generously and passionately served his country, his province, his constituency and, certainly, his Party.
It is unfortunate that political life be such that Jean came to the conclusion that he would tender his resignation to you this morning.
I got to know Jean at university, one of the Liberal students during the years from 1953 to 1960, and we have always been very close friends.
His departure will create a vacuum in the Commons, the Liberal Party is losing a dedicated worker in the House and, I repeat, I will miss him very much in Parliament.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD

speakeroldname: Hon. Robert de Cotret (President of the Treasury Board):
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, today I am pleased to table the Main Estimates for the fiscal year 1986-87 which amount to $107 billion, an increase of 4.4 per cent over the 1985-86 Main Estimates.
With the additional $500 million expenditure cut-back announced yesterday by my colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), which is not included in these estimates, the growth rate decreases to 3.9 per cent, the lowest rate recorded for the estimates in 24 years.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Of the total Main Estimates roughly two-thirds, or $69.5 billion, represents expenditures made in accordance with existing legislation, while the remaining $37.5 billion represents expenditures which Parliament is being asked to vote or authorize. It is this $37.5 billion over which the Government has the most direct control in the short and medium term and which most clearly indicates that the Government is determined to cut costs.
I am pleased to announce that for the second year in a row the rate of growth in these expenditures is virtually zero.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Taking into account the $500 million reduction, this growth rate is two-tenths of 1 per cent, the same as last year. Obviously, in real terms, once adjusted for inflation, this represents a reduction of roughly 4 per cent in these expenditures. This is the first time since the immediate postKorean War period that such a low rate of growth in the Government's operating expenditures has been achieved two years in a row.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
This very modest growth rate stands in sharp contrast to what this country has seen in the past. Indeed, over the period 1970 to 1984 the average annual growth rate in the voted portion of the Main Estimates well exceeded 10 per cent. In fiscal year 1975-76 it even reached a high of 36.8 per cent. It was no coincidence that such a situation prompted the then Auditor General to declare in his report for the fiscal year ended March 31, 1976, that:
-Parliament-and indeed the Government-has lost or is close to losing, effective control of the public purse.

Mr. Speaker, I have already referred to the low growth rate of the annual estimates, and I should emphasize that it has
Statements by Ministers
been achieved in spite of significant increases in expenditures for national defence and external aid to meet our international commitments. If we take the $500 million reduction into account, expenditures in all other operational sectors decline by 4.2 per cent on average, and this is in addition to last year's 2 per cent decrease.
This Government is intent on slashing expenditures, but in a reasonable manner. Last year when the Main Estimates were tabled we were forecasting total expenditures of $105 billion for 1985-86, including supplementary estimates. Although it had to cope with a number of major and unforeseen outlays, the Government now expects real expenditures of less than $104 billion for 1985-86. In fact, never since 1979-80 have total expenditures fallen below forecast levels, as they will this year.

This achievement was made possible as a result of a series of major undertakings over the past 18 months on a number of fronts, all designed to fulfil the Government's goal of managing the public sector more efficiently and more effectively, of doing more with less. All of this without reducing the high quality of our services to the public. More specifically, these low growth Main Estimates result from the tough measures we have undertaken to reduce government spending. During this time the Government has: first, streamlined or eliminated a number of costly or outdated programs, such as the Canada Oil Substitution Program, reduced business subsidies provided through DRIE and phased out Canagrex. Second, we have reduced business subsidies to many Crown corporations and privatized others. Third, we have eliminated the provision for inflation in Government operating budgets. Fourth, we have developed new cash management policies to reduce borrowing. Fifth, we have improved the management and control of Crown real estate. Finally, we have eliminated a five-year program to reduce the size and cost of the Public Service.
On this last point, the Estimates I tabled today show a reduction of some 5,500 person-years, or 2.1 per cent from the previous year for the year to come. This alone will save $150 million in 1986-87. By 1990 the reduction will total, as has been mentioned previously, 15,000 person-years. The accumulated savings to taxpayers will be $1.5 billion. The recurring annual savings will be approximately $500 million.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
As I have mentioned on previous occasions, every effort is being made to minimize the effect on employees and lay-offs, if any, will be kept to a minimum.

Over-all, the measures taken so far will make it possible to reduce projected expenditures or to earn non-tax revenues of about $6 billion in 1985-86 and $8 billion in 1986-87, as compared with the projected expenditures when the Government took office. I might add that such measures were taken

February 27, 1986
Statements by Ministers
after due consideration and that everything has been done to properly define the restraint sectors.
As I just said, yesterday the Minister of Finance announced a $500 million cut-back in expenditures for 1986-87. Treasury Board officials are now advising the various departments about these lower expenditures. However these restraint measures will be flexible enough so as not to harm the health and safety sectors, public services and programs for underprivileged Canadians. This is why reductions will differ from one department to another, overaping 2 per cent of voted expenditures.
The implementation of those measures has not been easy, Mr. Speaker. The success achieved until now points to the determination of all of my colleagues and to the support of higher echelons in the Public Service. Other challenges will have to be met as the management of expenditures remains a major component of this Government's strategy for controlling the deficit.
We realize that we have put and are putting a heavy burden on our managers and they responded well. Yesterday the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) announced that this year there will be no regular annual increase in the salaries of Deputy Ministers, Assistant Deputy Ministers and equivalent political staff. For the lower levels of the management category, salary ranges will be increased by up to 2 per cent only. We felt that this measure was essential to demonstrate the seriousness of our fiscal position. I am pleased to be able to say, however, that we shall continue to reward performance in our management category.
I shall soon announce a new feature in our management compensation package, a productivity bonus, which will reward those managers and Departments that meet and exceed their expenditure reduction targets while achieving their other program and policy goals.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: There will now be an inducement to rational economies with an appropriate reward system. It is our intention to reward excellence in management in a manner never before attempted in the federal Public Service.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: To conclude, Mr. Speaker, good management and reasoned reductions in expenditures over the last 18 months have given unprecedented results. This Budget shows the huge amount of success achieved by the Government in implementing its strategy. Our continuing efforts to restrain expenditures and improve management efficiency and effectiveness confirm this Government's sound leadership.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, this will not take very long, I can assure you. I know you are going to limit me to the time the Minister took, undoubtedly. I can see why his remarks were so short. Tory times are hard times.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
What is amazing about the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) and the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is that they are somehow trying to blame and punish the Canadian people for a problem that they themselves created.
When we examine the official record, we discover that in the past 17 months, the Government has managed to contribute 23 per cent to the total public debt of this nation. That is the exact Figure. The Minister of Finance on the one hand derides the previous administration and then on the other says that our payment on the debt has risen from $18 billion when the Government took over to $26 billion today. Obviously this is a Government of absolute contradictions.
A moment ago, the President of the Treasury Board said that we are now going to have a productivity bonus to pay to managers who save money for the federal Government. Although the President of the Treasury Board did not say it, 1 suppose this is meant for expenditures that are not fixed. However, by the same token, if they are not for those expenditures, then they will affect contractual employees and parttime help, and as well they will effect a saving to the federal treasury by having paid by the Government a bonus called a productivity bonus to save money for the Government. That in itself is absolutely and totally outrageous.
Looking at the facts again, I see that the Prime Minister's Office is still up in the high $6 million bracket for operations. 1 can see that spending in the Privy Council Office is up over $1 million. The Government allows that kind of extravagance but then turns around and tells Canadians that when they go to National Parks they have to go on self-guided tours because the Government can no longer afford tour guides. The Government then turns around and says it now has to pay out $900 million to provide a guarantee that was not there before for people with money in the bank. The Government then turns around and discontinues, through these Estimates, guarantees to primary producers. That is what I call a Government of total contradiction.
This Government has made more political appointments than any other administration, yet it is asking the Canadian public to approve a plan of bonus payments to civil servants who chop money for the federal treasury. In short, this is a disastrous Budget and a disastrous set of Estimates. When this sinks in, Canadians are not going to be pleased with the Minister of Finance and the President of the Treasury Board.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the Budget package and now the Estimates which have been laid before the House today seem to be designed to send a signal to financiers and bankers on Wall Street, Bay Street and in

financial markets around the world. Whatever the impact may be on business circles, I suggest that they also send a signal to ordinary Canadians and average Canadian families that the Government intends to fight the deficit on the backs of the average Canadian taxpayers.
The Government is fighting the deficit in this way, and it is doing it to the extent that next year corporate tax receipts for the Government of Canada will be down by $75 million while at the same time the Government expects to collect $7 billion more in sales taxes and income taxes from individuals. That is true. The President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) is shaking his head, but the fact is that for high income earners the tax rate will actually come down. For corporations, the tax rate will come down. It is the little guy who is going to be paying the cost of bringing down the deficit.
In terms of spending, it is also clear that the policy of the Government is to squeeze and squeeze regardless of the impact on ordinary Canadians. I remind the Government that there are a million and a quarter Canadians out there who are still unemployed, yet it is cutting back in the area of Canada Employment commission services and will be cutting the Canadian Jobs Strategy next year from $900 million to $800 million. Also I remind the Government that there are many Canadians who live in many places in this very large and widespread country, yet $70 million is to be taken out of the subsidies for weekly newspapers, other newspapers and magazine mailings across the country. Of course this will have a very direct impact upon the ability of Canadians to communicate with each other. It is something which we have had in the country for a hundred years, and for very good reasons- because of the nature of and the distances in our country. To take it away in the interest of reducing the deficit may please Wall Street, but it will be very difficult for average Canadians.
The Government projects a decrease of $200 million in the postal deficit, not in the five years projected by the March-ment Commission but in the course of one year beginning one month and one day from today. That will mean substantial cuts in services, substantial lay-offs and substantial increases in postal costs. Once again I suggest that they are neither appropriate nor affordable in terms of the services Canadians expect from the Post Office in a country as geographically vast as Canada.
Because the Government is more interested in acting tough than realistically coming to grips with the problems, we have the Government demonstrating that it can throw gore on the floor to the bankers and the financiers, regardless of whether there are other ways by which the necessary targets could be achieved.
In Cape Breton, where last year's measures have been totally useless, the Government has decided to cut back capital spending and is to defer the reconstruction of the Prince Mine coal washing plant, another major job-creating investment in Cape Breton which has been cut by the Government. Perhaps the President of the Treasury Board is not aware that we have
Statements by Ministers
20 per cent unemployed in Newfoundland, 15 per cent in New Brunswick, 13 per cent in British Columbia and 12 per cent in Quebec. However, spending on regional development is being cut once again. The economic and regional development package under the Conservatives is being cut by some $7 billion, if I understand it correctly, under the Government. It is a sign of the commitment of a Government which campaigned on the platform of jobs, jobs, jobs just 18 months or 20 months ago.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: That is what we delivered.

speakerposition: Parliamentary Secretary to the President of the Treasury Board
subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: Yes, 580,000 more jobs.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
There are a million and a quarter people unemployed out there. The Budget says that the unemployment rate will stay the same. It says that there are many people who will not get jobs. If the Government considered jobs a priority, it would bring the unemployment rate down to 7 per cent, to 6 per cent or to 5 per cent, not 10 per cent. It would bring down the unemployment rate in Newfoundland, New Brunswick and British Columbia, not just in central Canada.
The Government has a policy which says that the private sector is good and the public sector is bad. Somehow Conservatives just do not like Government at all. It is a bit like 1984-public sector bad, private sector good. Therefore we are seeing privatization and public sector services being cut back. We are seeing Government being treated as a scapegoat and therefore public servants in particular being treated as if they were responsible for what is happening, rather than being the victims of Government policy.
Women in particular will be the victims of the Government's policies. This morning we asked the Deputy Secretary of the Treasury Board whether there was any policy to ensure that women would not be unduly the victims of the Public Service cut-backs. "No, we have not thought of that", he said. There have been no directives coming from the political level of Government to ensure that the proportions laid off do not contain a disproportionate number of women. The evidence from Fisheries and other Departments is that a higher proportion of women are being cut back. I call upon the President of the Treasury Board to reverse that particular policy and announce it today.
Vital services are already being cut because of the $150 million cuts in the Public Service which have already been announced. The Government is cutting the Health and Welfare library. A valuable and irreplaceable national resource will be closed. Translation services, which are essential to Government in a bilingual country, are being cut back. Customs officers who, among other things, protect the country from the influx of drugs and pornography from abroad are being cut back. Canada Employment offices which help unemployed Canadians are being cut back in terms of the services which they can provide. Now the Government is taking a further step; we are told that in addition $500 million in non-statutory areas or almost four times as much will be cut.

February 27, 1986
Statements by Ministers
If the Government wanted the co-operation of public employees in making these cuts, it had ample room-and it has been demonstrated that it had ample room-to provide the job security protection which they sought and gain that cooperation. The 700 people which the President of the Treasury Board says will be cut back represent three-tenths of one per cent of the Public Service. If the pay agreement with the unions had been cut back by three-tenths of one per cent-and I am sure they would have accepted that-the money could have been found to save those 700 people from being thrust into a difficult job market. This does not only affect Ottawa, it affects the whole country. If the Government can find $500 million in the cuts announced in the Budget yesterday, it could have found the necessary sums to have kept those 700 jobs, allowing any changes in the Public Service to have taken place by attribution, not by the cuts which are now taking place.
The Government wanted to demonstrate to bankers that it could fire, that it could be tough, that it could be rough, just like back in the 1890s on the 1920s. That is what it wanted to do.
[ Translation]
This is what this Government attempted to do. They wanted to show the financial community that they were a tough Government, that they were capable of laying off secretaries, clerks, messengers, women and other groups that are now being laid off because of this Government's policy. This is simply in order to make a show of their toughness, not because it is needed in terms of budget or fiscal policy.

I ask how the Public Service can work effectively with these policies from the President of the Treasury Board. People will not be prepared to co-operate if they fear that in co-operating they will in fact be jeopardizing their own jobs. The Government has not abandoned the archaic, out of date policy of exercising reverse order of merit and making arbitrary decisions in terms of who goes and who stays. Public employees who have been in office for 20 years and have worked hard are being dumped, while people working in the same office with them, having been there for five years, are being kept. That is clearly unfair, unkind, unwise and ill-advised.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext: And untrue.

subtopic: EXPLANATORY STATEMENT BY PRESIDENT OF THE TREASURY BOARD
speechtext:
I want to make a couple of specific proposals. In the first place we were told by the deputy secretary today that the $500 million in cuts would not include further cuts in the Public Service. I suggest that that $500 million could lead to as many as 10,000 more cuts in the Public Service. There must be a better process of monitoring than has been announced up to now. I suggest very specifically to the President of the Treasury Board that the $500 million worth of cuts should be referred to the standing committees of the House of Commons which now have the responsibility of departmental oversight under the new rules that came into force at the beginning of this week when we returned from the break. I
make that suggestion quite constructively and positively to the President of the Treasury Board.
In addition, now we know that 6,151 jobs will be cut; 1,000 in Defence, 623 in Transport, 549 in Public Works, 455 in Supply and Services, 393 in National Health and Welfare, 376 in Agriculture, 374 in Indian Affairs, 296 in Energy, Mines and Resources, and so it goes. At last we have the list. We need a means of monitoring to ensure that those cuts are not being applied unfairly as is shown by the evidence right now. If those cuts have to be made, I want the President of the Treasury Board to ensure on behalf of the Government that they will in fact be monitored and surveyed by the standing committees for each Department, rather than allow arbitrary and unfair cuts to be made by Public Service managers who will be rewarded with productivity bonuses the more efficiently and the tougher they appear in making those cuts.

The Budget-Mr. Johnston
that this House approves in general the budgetary policy of the Government.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to rise again this morning after having had the opportunity of offering a few preliminary comments and impressions with respect to the Budget presented by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) in this House yesterday.
I might say that the Minister who is with us at present has had the courtesy to inform me that he will be leaving the Chamber. It is because of another appointment and not because of anything that I am about to say, although I suspect in his heart of hearts he would probably be in agreement with most of my statements and the conclusions at which 1 have arrived.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Oh, oh!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
To begin, I said last night that 1 would take some time between yesterday evening and this morning to examine the Budget to see what I could find in it that might be of value. Unfortunately, some of the lesser areas which will be of benefit to particular taxpayers really do not fit into my speech today, but I will comment on them in due course.
1 must say over-all I can summarize my impressions of the Budget with five adjectives. First, as 1 said last night, 1 believe the Budget is cowardly. I know you corrected me yesterday, Mr. Speaker, when you said I could not refer to people as cowardly, but I am not referring to the Minister of Finance as a coward, I am referring to the Budget itself. Second, 1 think it is appropriate to say that the Budget is grossly unfair. Third, the Budget is deceitful in the way it was presented and crafted. The Budget could be described as short-sighted. It could also be described as unimaginative, and finally, it could be described as economically unsound.

This morning, Mr. Speaker, I would like to take a few minutes to discuss each one of these issues: the economy, the question of equity, etc. As you know-
It is cowardly because instead of bringing forward the Nielsen Task Force report and examining those areas where cuts could be made-
[Translation[
Instead of cutting Government programs, the Minister has chosen to launch an attack on Canadian taxpayers. He has decided not to slash his programs, perhaps with the Prime Minister's encouragement, but first and foremost to launch an attack against taxpayers for the reason that they cannot defend themselves.

I recall, Mr. Speaker, and 1 am sure that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) does because I have reminded him of it a number of times, the interview that he gave to Question

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
Period, I think on March 1, 1985, in the pre-Budget period. In response to a question by Mr. Terry Wills of The Gazette as to whether he would increase taxes, the Minister said that taxes are not the way to go, that there is enough room on the expenditure side. He said that on March 1. Then, as we know, in May of last year he brought in the heaviest tax bill that this country has ever witnessed in peace time.
What happened to the Minister of Finance who appeared on Question Period? With all due respect to the Minister, for whom I have high regard, I suggest that he lost his battle in Cabinet, that he lost to his colleagues and especially the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney), and that he was unable to bring forward the Budget which he wanted. He did not want to impose the greatest tax burden that Canadians have ever suffered.
Yesterday the Minister had the unmitigated gall to stand in the House with the Budget in front of him, which again exacerbated the tax bill, and tell the people of Canada, "the buck stops here". What a laugh. I would like to see him say that with a straight face to the average Canadian taxpayer. They know where the buck stops. The buck stops in their pocketbooks, that is where the buck stops. They wanted it to stop with the Minister and with the Government, but no, Sir, the buck stops with them. They know exactly where the buck stops.
How big a buck has stopped in their pocketbooks? For the year 1986-87 alone the Minister has added $560 million in personal surtax, a sales tax bill of $815 million, a tobacco tax of $150 million, and corporate taxes. The total bill comes to $1,905 billion. That is the buck that stopped yesterday in the pocketbooks of the taxpayers of Canada. Adding to that the taxes imposed in May of last year, which come to a grand total of $4,380 billion, the total for 1986-87 is $6,285 billion. That means that each taxpayer will have to pay approximately $628 of additional federal income tax. Next year the story will repeat itself. Next year there will be an additional $3 billion added to the $4 billion from last May, which is a total in excess of $7 billion in 1987-88.
We do not have all the data for the intervening years until 1990-91 because the Government has once again failed to live up to the obligations imposed upon us by the Lambert Commission, which we honoured, to give detailed five-year projections. Therefore, we have a hiatus in the numbers which were offered. In any event, in 1990-91 there will be total of $13.25 billion more in taxes suffered by the people of Canada. That is where the buck stops. It did not stop with the Government. That is what Canadian taxpayers have been asked to bear.
The Minister has slapped himself on the back about all his spending restraint saying that historically no Government has ever done such a thing. I would wager, Mr. Speaker, that there have never ever been tax increases of this magnitude in peace time in the history of the country.
Let us suppose for a moment that the Government was simply going to hold its spending to the 1985-86 level. Is that asking a lot? That would mean that in 1986-87, instead of increasing spending to $116,740 billion, spending could have
remained at $112,250 billion. That would have simply been holding the line. Canadian taxpayers want to know why the Government is not holding the line. The difference is $4,490 billion. Had the Government held the line, that amount would have been available to apply against the deficit. A simple calculation shows that without any additional taxes the deficit would have been further reduced to $26,880 billion. That would have happened without any tax increases at all. If the Minister had held the line and not increased spending, he could have risen to slap himself on the back in the House and proudly say, "the buck stops here". But the buck did not stop here, it was passed on to Canadian taxpayers.
It is cowardly that the Minister and the Prime Minister are not willing to face individual Canadian constituents, but are quite prepared to face the Third World. They are quite prepared to lop $1.5 billion from our foreign aid over the next five years. In his presentation and in the budget documents the Minister points out that Canada is still better than France, the United States, and Britain in terms of the percentage of Gross National Product devoted to foreign aid. However, he neglected to mention that those countries rank between tenth and twelfth on the list of donors and that Canada ranks ninth. In fact,there are eight industrialized countries which make substantially higher contributions to foreign aid than does Canada.
Therefore, he has no reason to slap himself on the back. In fact, he has reason to be deeply shamed, as has the Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) who has responsibility to ensure that that Budget is maintained and that Canada meets the targets which have been set. The target of .6 per cent has now been postponed until 1995. That also contradicts an earlier statement made by the Secretary of State that he would like to have the target increased to .7 per cent.
I do not think that the Minister understands what is happening to ordinary Canadians. You may have seen The Journal last night. On that program some middle-income families in Ajax, Ontario, were interviewed. I thought it was a very good use of television, especially since the Minister of Finance was obliged to sit and watch the direct impact of his Budget on the lives of ordinary Canadians.
One of the gentlemen interviewed in that program talked about his house that he had renovated and worked for. He said, "You know, I own only 25 per cent of my house, the bank owns the other three-quarters". He said, "I have no place to find these funds. I feel that I'm going behind". They all felt that they were going behind. The Minister of Finance when he was subsequently interviewed said, yes, he had empathy and sympathy for these people. He referred to the man with the house ownership problem, and with the big mortgage that absorbed, if you like, three-quarters of the equity value of his house, and he said, "Canada is in the same boat". He seized upon that example to draw a parallel between the circumstances of the country and the circumstances of the individual
February 27, 1986

who is burdened with a mortgage on his home and only has a 25 per cent equity interest. It is not the same thing.
Who does that gentleman we watched on television last night turn to to protect his investment, to pay off his debt? Who does he turn to? We know who the Government of Canada turns to. The Government of Canada is turning to that gentleman, to the taxpayers of Canada. The buck stops with him. He has nowhere to go. He can go to his employer and seek a raise, but if he is not successful I suggest he will go further and further into debt. The Government of Canada simply issues a writ asking us to contribute billions of dollars to its coffers. I suggest the buck is passed. It doesn't stop here, it stops there with those families in Ajax and with families like that right across this country.
Why did the Minister decide to take the easy way out? Why did he decide simply to clobber middle-income and lower-income Canadians? That is the unfair part of this Budget. Having decided to tax why did he tax in such an unfair manner? You may recall the Minister declared not too many months ago that this country suffered from an acute shortage of rich people. With this Minister and this Government there certainly will not be any increase in the number of rich people. In fact, we seem to be on our way to wiping out the middle class. He still is a supply-sider. You may recall last year I talked about the horse and sparrow economics of John Kenneth Galbraith. The theory that if you feed the horse enough that something will be left over for the sparrows. The Minister is not only practising supply side economics by maintaining the capital gains exemption, by reducing the surtax for upper-income Canadians he in fact is going to wipe out the sparrows. It is not even horse and sparrow economics, it is worse. He is still feeding the horse; the capital gains exemption is still there, and in addition to that he is hitting middle and lower-income Canadians.
Mr. Speaker, let me read you a few headlines which really say it all in terms of the fairness of this Budget:
Ordinary earners hit hardest again.
From The Globe and Mail:
When you are middle class, it is a struggle to stay there.
Next headline from The Globe and Mail:
Individual taxpayers cannon fodder in three-pronged assault on deficit.

There was also this headline in La Presse:
The 3 per cent surtax will hurt the individuals.

Another one, Mr. Speaker, again from The Globe:
Middle-income earners will carry bulk of new load.
Then it says:
Surtax less costly than at present for those at high end of the scale.
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
There you are, feeding the horse and attacking the sparrows. The next one:
Happy investors keep exemption on capital gains.
Finally ...

And I quote: "Wilson missed the mark", wrote Alain Dubuc in La Presse. So that is how the Budget is described. There is the clear message given by headlines in today's newspapers.
In conclusion, I would like to quote from Mr. Dubuc's comments: "After all those expectations, the Minister of Finance did a near tour de force by tabling a dumb and unimaginative Budget. The only positive note is that he just about brought the deficit under the $30 billion mark".
Clearly, Mr. Speaker, our Minister missed his shot.

I also said that the Budget was deceitful. Let me take you to page 20 of the budget speech.

-the Minister suggested yesterday, under the heading "Research and Development":
A second priority is investment in knowledge.
The crucial importance of knowledge to Canada's future requires a new partnership between the private and public sectors. The federal Government plays a major role in supporting university-based research and the development of highly qualified personnel in Canada. One channel for this support is through the operations of the Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council, the Medical Research Council and the Social Sciences and Humanities Research Council. The Government proposes to provide a secure funding base for these councils by adding S300 million over the balance of the decade.

In fact, one would have thought that this followed upon the grand declarations of our now Prime Minister in his book, Where / Stand, when he attacked the Liberal Government of the day for what he considered a lack of interest in research and development. I quote from page 41 of the book:
If the percentage of GNP allocated to research and development were increased by 1 per cent we could create in Canada one million new jobs and $20 billion in additional sales of manufactured products.
Now, that was in the book Where l Stand. The next edition will be called "where I stood".

Because, clearly, our Prime Minister's feet (Mr. Mulroney) are made of clay.

That being said, one would have thought, as some journalist did, that the Government was really giving a boost to research and development in this country, $300 million. I turn here to The Gazette which says:
Research Councils received $300-million boost.
Let me refer you to the five-year plan of only one of those councils referred to in the Minister's speech. Take this particular council, because when I was Minister of Science and Technology I had responsibility for the council, which is the

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
Natural Sciences and Engineering Research Council known under the acronym of NSERC. A five-year plan was presented to the Government, and during the period from 1984-85 to 1989-90 the plan requires $1.4 billion in increased funding in 1984-85 constant dollars.
The Government has offered NSERC the Medical Research Council and the Social Science and Humanities Council $300 million to be divided among them. This is supposed to be a great coup. This is supposed to be a boost in research and development.
In this report we find a number of statements which are important. I read from page 202 of the five-year plan of the council as follows:
The initiatives proposed by the second Five-Year Plan are based on the established, well-proven and highly-accepted programs of NSERC and represent an urgent investment opportunity for the federal Government. Given the key role they play in providing for the future of R&D in Canada, their rejection would be tantamount to a rejection of not only the national targets, but also of the economic activity that can only come from a more sophisticated and technologically oriented society. Surely that option of retreat is not a valid one even in today's environment of fiscal restraint.
My goodness, we have not only seen retreat, we have seen a virtual abandonment of this plan. The treatment this Council is receiving, I suggest, is shocking in the extreme. We know that even to provide for inflationary increases and stay even, NSERC alone would require $380 million over that period. But the Government offers $300 million to the three councils and pretends that this is a great step forward in stimulating research and development in Canada.
[ Translation]
Frankly, Mr. Speaker, ever since this Government has come to power, identifying its priorities has been very difficult. When we look at the bailout of the two banks that went bankrupt-$2 billion-and compare that with the circumstances of those councils, in the area of research and development, truly, I understand absolutely nothing about the goals and directions the Government would like to pursue.

This Government, I suggest, is rooted in the economy of 20 years ago and does not understand that the kind of growth which is necessary to get the deficit under control comes from a heavier and greater commitment to research and development, technology and productivity.
This brings me to another one of my adjectives. I said the Budget was "shortsighted". It is indeed shortsighted for the reasons I have just listed in terms of research and development. If there is one place we do not want to cut, it is in that area. We have to improve the intellectual capital. That is where the future of Canada lies. This Budget is a direct assault on that objective.
Something else about which one could make a speech for days is the question of foreign aid-talk about shortsightedness. We who have studied the potential problems in this biosphere know that the greatest problem will not be East-
West. That has to be controlled, and must be controlled, but lying there as a sleeping time bomb is the North-South. That is a problem which this country has a proud record in addressing. We know that unless the standards of living of the third world are raised, the population explosion itself will create demands upon this planet which we will not be able to support by the year 2050. I know that is long-term thinking and that this Government does not consider long-term thinking especially significant. This Government really does not think beyond the next election. That is readily apparent from certain aspects of this Budget. However, I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that we shall pay dearly not only as Canadians but as Members of the international community on this planet earth if we start to reject the responsibilities towards the Third World and the North-South dialogue which we have so readily accepted in the past. This Government, for short-term gain, has set about to cut into the Budget to the tune of $1.5 billion over the next five years.
In addition, I said that this is an unimaginative Budget. Monsieur Dubuc in La Presse makes that point. It does not really require genius, does it, to impose millions of dollars in taxes? I would have thought that any of us here, even without any economic knowledge whatsoever, would say: "If additional funds are required, why don't we increase sales taxes or personal income taxes?" That seems to be the obvious thing to do. That does not require any genius. It does not even require a Minister of Finance. But that is what we have and that is why the Budget is completely unimaginative. Stacked upon the taxes which were imposed last May, not only is it unimaginative, it is economically counter-productive.
The cuts talked about by the Government, for the most part, are not real. They are ghost cuts, as some commentators have described them, but the taxes are very real. We will pay the taxes but the cuts are theoretical numbers. For example, Mr. Speaker, if you went to the Government and said you were going to spend $6,000 on a round-the-world trip and then a day later you said you had decided to go to Florida and it will only cost you $1,500 and you have saved $4,500, the Government would say: "Yes, you have cut your Budget by $4,500". That is the kind of cuts we are talking about in most instances.
As I demonstrated at the outset, the Government has proved itself incapable of holding the line, let alone cutting into expenses. Our expenses are increasing at the rate of billions of dollars per year. They are moving from $112 billion to $116 billion, as I mentioned. But the taxes are real, and in imposing these taxes discretionary spending and necessary spending is being cut to the detriment of the pocket books of Canadians. Canadian men, women and children, if I can go back to my earlier analogy of Galbraith, are the "sparrows" who are suffering.
The Budget has to be inflationary. I said that in May of 1985. I know that some people have said that it has not been inflationary because inflation is still at 4.4 per cent. However, we know that the impact of a Budget is somewhere between eight months, 12 months and sometimes 15 months down the road. You may not be aware of this, Mr. Speaker, but inflation
February 27, 1986

in this country over the last three months is running at 5.6 per cent. If we were to project that forward, we would have an annual rate of 5.6 per cent.
Our neighbours to the south do use a forward projection for certain purposes. We do not. We always reduce the rate of inflation, or increase it, by past experience. The only true test is to look at what is happening now and what is happening now is that we have a 5.6 rate of inflation. I suggest to you, Mr. Speaker, that with the burden of taxes we are putting on consumers, the price of gasoline and the price of food is going to increase that rate of inflation, expecially when it is combined with the weak dollar delivered to us by this Government.
I mentioned the people from Ajax whom we saw on television. What will they and the workers of this country from coast-to-coast do when faced with these tax increases? Will they not try to pass the buck as well? Should they not be entitled to pass the buck? How will they pass the buck? The only means at their disposal is to ask for higher wages. Their only recourse is to increase wage demands. I would say that the workers have been very responsible since the six and five program was introduced by the Liberal Government back in 1982. But I say to you, Mr. Speaker, that when we impose taxes of this kind on goods which they require to maintain their standards of living, they will feel they are justified in asking for higher wages. That is how the inflationary spiral starts. That is how the CPI increases, which in turn is why interest rates can increase and are likely to increase.
If savers continue to demand a real rate of interest at the levels we have seen over the past year, how on earth are interest rates going to come down? How will they come down faced as we are with the incredible tax increases and inflationary impact in this Budget? If interest rates creep up or even stay at their present level, which is much too high in the circumstances-they went up to defend the dollar but may stay up now because of the Budget-the economy is likely to grow more slowly. There will be fewer jobs and, of course, there will be higher taxes. These matters are known to the Minister of Finance and to the Minister of State for Finance (Mrs. McDougall) who I am pleased to see here with us today. They know they are vulnerable and they know, of course, that their $29.5 billion deficit number is equally vulnerable.
The whole Budget proceeds on a number of assumptions. 1 am not going to attack the assumptions. I just want to raise certain questions with respect to them which I would like the Minister of Finance and the Minister of State for Finance to reflect upon. First, there is the assumption that it is inflationary, a point which I have already made. That is a serious matter. I continue to regard another round of inflation as public enemy No. 1. Nothing could throw our economy into a decline as quickly as indications that we will have more inflation-and this Budget is inflationary.
There are also other assumptions. For example, there is the assumption that oil prices over the next two years will be in the neighbourhood of $22.50 per barrel. We know that the spot
The Budget-Mr. Johnston
price at present is much lower than that. It seems that the Minister of Finance and his colleagues must be praying that the price will rise to the neighbourhood of $22.50 per barrel. There is a rule of thumb in this respect with which Hon. Members may be familiar. That is to say, each one dollar reduction in the price of oil represents a loss of revenue to the federal Government of approximately $110 million. In fact, the Economic Council of Canada has indicated that if the price of oil is $19 a barrel-and it is much lower than that on the spot market now-there will be a loss of $500 million to the Treasury. That is one assumption, a terribly fragile one, with very little evidence which any of us can see to support it. The $29.5 billion deficit and everything which flows from it is predicated upon such an assumption.
Another assumption is that interest rates this year will be at 9.5 per cent and will fall off next year to something in the order of 8.7 per cent. That means that we will have to see a reduction in interest rates-let us hope that we will see such a reduction. I have raised a number of concerns with respect to pressures which the Government has placed on the system which may, indeed, make such a reduction impossible. The Minister of Finance, and I presume the Minister of State for Finance are praying for a fall in interest rates. Let us hope that their prayers will be answered. I must say that I am skeptical in that regard.
I cannot help but add one last cynical comment. In some respects this Budget strikes me as a pre-election Budget. The Government seems to be saying: "Let's really sock it to them in 1986. Let's make those taxpayers really pay and then let's have some softening around 1988 just before the next general election". The Government will probably broaden the sales tax or it will come forward with a VAT or a business transfer tax in the next Budget. There are indications of that in the Budget documents. The Government probably plans to remove the personal surtax.
My colleagues and I would like to give the Government some advice in this regard. The Canadian electorate is too smart for this type of gamesmanship. It is not prepared to pay to have its standard of living suffer just to meet the electoral timetable of the Government. We will remind Canadians constantly-that is if they need any reminding at all-of what the Government did to them in 1985 in terms of unfairness and in terms of the tax burden itself, and what the Government is planning for them in the years ahead. We will be here to remind them.
We have no confidence in the Government's fiscal management of the country. The Budget has been a profound disappointment.

As 1 said yesterday in the House, I was disappointed last year. In fact, I am even more disappointed today, because I think there is a lack of imagination in this Budget. It is very poorly planned, very poorly designed, and it is now putting an intolerable burden on the taxpayers of this country.

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Riis
[English)
Therefore, I move, seconded by the Right Hon. Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner):
That the motion of the Minister of Finance be amended by deleting all of the words after the word "That" and by substituting the following:
"this House condemns the Government for presenting a Budget that imposes outrageous and unfair tax increases for ordinary Canadians that deliberately widen the gap between them the rich and poor and between the "have" and "have-not" regions of this country."

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will take the motion under advisement and call upon the next speaker from the New Democratic Party. The Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis).

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is a pleasure to have an opportunity to respond to this incredible Budget. I suspect the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) is sitting, cringing in his seat, knowing that some reality will finally unfold in terms of what the Budget means to the average, ordinary Canadian family which has been bludgeoned by his Budget. It has been sugar-coated all right. There are all types of measures in the Budget which first give the appearance that it is a fair Budget. I have actually heard some individuals from the media-people whom I normally respect for their views-say that it is a fair budget. If anyone has read the Budget, then I cannot believe that they would say it is fair. They have probably merely scanned the booklet which sets out the Budget in brief and which highlights some of the sugar-coating.
When one looks carefully at the Budget one will see that the people of Canada have really been misled over the last number of years. On behalf of the New Democratic Party I hope to shed some light on what the Budget really does to the people of Canada.
In order to put the matter into context let us recognize that as we speak today about the Budget there are 4.5 million people in the country who are living below the poverty line. I refer to the poverty line as described and defined by the Government. As we speak there are 1.4 million jobless Canadians. There are hundreds of thousands of young people who are out of work and who are not in colleges or universities. They are jobless and are giving up in terms of ever having a full-time and meaningful job, because in the regions of the country in which they live there is simply no economic growth and expansion taking place. In those regions of the country where new jobs come up people with experience and training are wanted to fill them. Of course, to a large extent, that excludes the young people of our country.
The people of Canada have been taxed to the hilt. The New Democratic Party has just completed a tour of the country, an exercise which we called Tax Probe 86. In this probe we were asking people about the tax system and what they felt about it. The feelings expressed have been absolutely unanimous. It does not matter to whom one speaks or where one speaks to them. Everyone in the country says that the tax system is
unduly complex, unfair and that it does not give the country good value for money. That feeling is unanimous.
Is there one thing in the Budget which indicates that the Government is serious about tax reform? No, there is nothing. As a matter of fact, if one were to look closely at the budget documents one would see that the tax system will be more complex than ever. It will be less fair than it has ever been. There is no mention of tax reform at a time when the Government says it needs more revenue. That is unconscionable. The fact that the Government failed to move on such an important issue at this point in time when the people of Canada would be behind the Government in terms of overhauling the tax system is a missed opportunity.
Let us take a look at the Budget. We have been here before. This is not the first time Canada has experienced difficulties. I would like to read two or three of what I think are appropriate quotes from the Budget. I encourage the Ministers present to reflect on the words of the Budget which are as follows:
Mr. Speaker, the general optimism prevailing throughout Canada has, during recent months, been so widely reflected and strongly emphasized in provincial legislative assemblies, annual reviews and financial statements that, in presenting this annual budget, little need be said beyond submitting official figures which, when analyzed and compared with the records of previous years, will show a steady and continuous reduction of... debt-
Without being unduly optimistic, the Government feels it is warranted in anticipating that, notwithstanding the reductions to be submitted in this budget, the revenues will meet all expenditure obligations and also provide for the redemption of the loan maturing in August next ... For the purposes of eventually effecting a balanced budget, provision was made in the budget... for certain additional taxation. The major increase was made in the sales tax where the rates were increased fifty per cent over the then existing tax. There was also an increase in the stamp tax... Certain other taxes, generally classed as manufacturers taxes, were imposed, the articles affected being automobiles, confectionery, cigars, ale and beer and other beverages:... The national debt, however, cannot be ignored. The annual interest charges... are a direct and pressing charge on the revenues of this country.
It is a sound and helpful policy to plan to reduce this non-productive outlay and to do that the national debt itself must annually be reduced. The government is, therefore, again budgeting for debt reduction ... the concern of all Canadians was... that the nation's purchasing power be substantially increased, that no man willing to work be out of employment, that Canadian goods become firmly established on the international trading markets and that Canadians, wherever they might be, would feel that the problems of each section were the mutual concern of all... Canadians today are prospering ... Our basic and manufacturing industries are producing large quantities of goods for home consumption and also for the vast external trade outlets which have been developed-
As the years go by an increasing quantity of our domestic production must necessarily be marketed abroad. It is our desire to trade freely with any and all who are willing to trade with us... This fiscal record ... has... strengthened confidence in our domestic credit markets, thus smoothing the way for the provinces and private enterprises. A healthy business expansion, the Government feels, is of the greatest importance to Canada.
In drafting the fiscal program for the coming fiscal year, the Government has sought to err on the side of caution.
What is interesting is that that was not this Budget, that was the Budget of March 1, 1929. That was the Budget that was introduced prior to the collapse of 1929. Later, of course, the R. B. Bennett Budget was introduced and the Government at the time said it had a great solution, it was going to raise taxes on everyone across the country to collect more revenue
February 27, 1986

and it was going to give some corporations some tax breaks and increase the sales tax. We know what happened in the 1930s as a result of that. Bennett buggies resulted. We have been here before. We have seen Conservative Budgets introduced during difficult times, and what happens? Do things get better? Do times get better?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tory times are tough times.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As my colleague has said, Tory times are tough times. We are about to experiment once again-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The dollar dropped three-quarters of a cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
My leader has told me that the dollar dropped three-quarters of a cent today. Is that not interesting? That reminds us that the Government is gambling with the lives of Canadian families. The Minister has launched a Las Vegas style approach to economic development. He said that we are going to gamble and raise sales taxes one more time even though it has already been done twice. He knows it is a regressive tax. It is a tax that hits the poorer families harder than the richer families. As a matter of fact, the richer families probably do not even notice the sales tax. The Government is going to level a regressive sales tax and jack up the personal tax rate again by 3 per cent.
By taking a lot of money out of the pockets of families across the country, the Government believes that somehow all sorts of money will start rolling into the country. Businesses will then begin expanding operations to take advantage of this new-found optimism and purchasing power, but there is no more purchasing power. When the Government takes disposable income away from people they are not going to buy a new refrigerator, a new car or go for dinner. They are going to err on the side of caution. They are going to be very reluctant to purchase goods and services. Without consumers purchasing goods and services, businesses will not expand and will not hire more people. The economy will not grow. Yet that is the gamble the Minister of Finance is taking on the backs of Canadian families; if we cut those programs that service Canadian families, somehow or other the international corporate and investment community will have confidence in the Government's ability to manage the economy and will feel that the economy will grow.
The first indicator we have seen is that the dollar is falling the day after the Budget was brought down. That sends a very clear signal to us about what the international community thinks about this Budget.
I think this can be best summed up when we look at the fiscal plan itself. The fiscal plan lays out what the Government is going to collect in new taxes. Here is the story, the story that Canadians across the country will be recognizing in the days ahead as the real Budget information comes out.
The additional taxes that Canadians are going to be paying either through more personal tax or more sales tax amounts to an increase of $7 billion between 1986 and 1987. What about the corporate sector? Someone said the Budget was fair. We
The Budget-Mr. Riis
would then assume that corporate-sector taxes would be going up. However, they are going to go down. The taxes collected from corporations in the next year will go down and the personal taxes paid by Canadians will go up by $7 billion.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Tory justice.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
It is a very, very sad day. However, this is misleading. When looking at particular aspects of the Budget, we see that $800 million will be allocated for the Canadian Jobs Strategy next year. That sounds interesting until we realize that this year it had $900 million in its budget. The Government is going to cut the funds for the Canadian Jobs Strategy. What does that mean for the regions of Canada? Job-creation funds might not be needed in many constituencies in the City of Toronto, but in the regions of Canada job-creation funds are an absolute necessity and the Government is cutting back on them.
Then there is a provision in the Budget for helping older workers, workers who are 55 and over and have lost their jobs. The Government is going to put $125 million into this program over the next four years. Again, that sounds like it would be a useful program. That amounts to about $30 million a year. However, we realize that presently the program receives $75 million a year. Again the Government is cutting programs to assist older workers who have lost their jobs.
There is a lot of sugar coating over this Budget, but when we start looking through it, we notice that there are some very disappointing aspects to it, particularly for the regions. The regional industrial expansion section of the Budget indicates that $2 billion will be cut over the next four years. How does that help the regions develop their economies? A $4-billion cut will cause serious damage.
Transportation will be cut by $3.6 billion. The employment part of the Budget will be cut by $1.8 billion. Agriculture is going to be cut by $502 million but there is a program introduced to help people get out of farming. The Government is cutting existing programs, but for those people who are having trouble it is helping them get out of the business. It is giving them an exit visa out of the farming community. That is what is in the Budget. The Government says that it has a program to help farmers who are in trouble. Approximately
50,000	farms across the country are experiencing serious financial difficulty, but they will only be helped if they are doing business with the Farm Credit Corporation, which amounts to about one in four troubled farmers. If a farmer is having trouble with the Royal Bank of Canada there is no help. If farmers have loans with chartered banks there is no assistance or possible support in the Budget. For those few farmers who are having difficulty in terms of repaying their debts or loans with the FCC, they will perhaps receive some support. It is a sugar-coating. I saw the little clips on television about assistance to farmers in trouble. They forgot to say that only one out of four farmers in trouble will possibly receive assistance.

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Riis
There is a 3 per cent decrease in corporate taxes over the next three years, but this coming year there will be a 3 per cent increase in personal taxes. Earlier today my Leader held a press conference and pointed out an interesting shift over the last few years. Not many years ago when we looked at the revenues collected from corporations and from individuals, there was a 50-50 balance-50 per cent of the revenues coming in through taxation was from corporations and 50 per cent was from individual Canadian taxpayers. Over the years this has shifted in a very interesting direction. Now 81 per cent comes from the personal tax side and 19 per cent comes from the corporate side.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: As a result of the Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Especially as a result of the Budget. It has simply added to the same process; more and more on the backs of middle-income earners and less and less on the backs of the corporate sector.
As we all know average Canadians will be faced with a 3 per cent increase in their taxes as well as an increase in sales tax. What about upper-income earners? They receive a reduced tax as a result of the Budget. Their tax rate goes down. The situation is that upper-income earners and the corporate sector will have reduced tax rates as a result of the Budget and ordinary Canadian taxpayers will experience increases in their tax rates and in the sales tax.
People are asking about the real impact of this, how it can be measured and what it really means. It does not take much analysis to break it down in terms of what this Government has meant to Canadian families. If we look at the November 8, 1985 statement and tally up the costs as a result of it on the average Canadian family-and I am using for this example an average Canadian family of four with an income of $35,000 per year-we find that it resulted in $452 in increased costs.
If we look at the May 23, 1985 Budget, we find that the increased costs to that same family as a result of the modification to indexation, the cut in family allowance payments, the increased taxes on cigarettes, alcohol and gasoline and the sales tax increase, amounted to $512.50. Then we have the Budget of February 26, yesterday. When we add up the costs as a result of it the very conservative total, if I may use that term, comes to $340. If we add up the totals as a result of that economic statement and those Budgets, we find that the increase from the federal Government alone amounts to $1,304.50 for an average Canadian family of four. It is the largest tax grab in modern history, in recent times.
We have never seen anything like this before, when a Government has gone in and ripped out more than $1,000 from Canadian families in just 14 months. This means that for every family in Canada-whether it be in Port Alberni, Red Deer, Thunder Bay, Chicoutimi, Moncton or St. Catharines, it does not matter where-in excess of $1,000 or $1,300 will not be circulating in those communities time and time again during the year to support the local economies. It has been
dragged out of those communities and down to Ottawa to be used for some highly questionable purposes.
What are those purposes? Let us look at how the tax system is used. We asked for a major overhaul of the tax system because we were convinced that the hidden spending which takes place through the shelters, loopholes and various tax expenditure programs comes to billions and billions of dollars each year, and they are never evaluated. We asked the Government to look at these tax expenditure programs and to evaluate them to see whether or not we are getting good value for the money. If we have a program which is designed to encourage the construction of low-income rental housing, is it doing that? Of course when we look at the program it never does that. Is the use of the tax system to encourage mining exploration the most effective way of accomplishing that? We have to ask these questions. Was there one mention of tax reform, tax overhaul or evaluating the value of those tax dollars in the Budget? Not a word, not a word.
Let us look at the incredible amount of money involved in the tax system. One of the favourite areas people mention is the amount of taxes known as deferred corporate taxes. It now approaches nearly $30 billion annually. Numbers of corporations do not pay; they simply defer their taxes year after year. Mr. Speaker, when you and I do not pay any income tax or make a mistake on our income tax return and owe money to the Government, we pay interest on it whether it is two weeks or two months.
