speechtext:
Just before the Budget was brought down, the New Democratic Party wanted to offer the Minister of Finance a whole set of suggestions about things he might do to help ordinary Canadians. We suggested that there should be an overhaul of the tax system and that a number of tax
February 27, 1986

programs should be eliminated immediately. At the top of the list was the $500,000 capital gains tax exemption, which means that a person who makes money from playing the stock market in Hong Kong or selling real estate in Arizona does not have to pay any income tax. At the same time the rates are being increased for ordinary Canadians. We suggested a number of tax measures which could have been eliminated and could have saved the Government about $3.5 billion. We suggested a number of recommendations to improve the tax system, for example, that the taxes on farm fuels and the like should be eliminated. We also looked at the result of our youth task force, the NDP task force on jobs and the report entitled "Canada Unlimited", which contained a number of recommendations on how the Government could take positive steps that could result in economic growth and expansion. We feel that the best way to collect revenue is not by taxing people more and more, but by taking steps to develop a strong and healthy economy.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
If we have a strong and healthy economy, then we have people who are not necessarily receiving UIC and welfare payments. They are paying more taxes in terms of personal taxes and sales tax. As well, successful businesses are paying corporate taxes and the Government is collecting excise taxes. A healthy economy results in revenues coming in to the Government for useful social programs, and if necessary part of it could be used to reduce the deficit. We would like to see the Government accumulate more revenue, and we have suggested a host of ways of doing it.
The Secretary of State for External Affairs (Mr. Clark) last September suggested at the UN that Canada would approach 0.7 of 1 per cent GNP by 1990, but this has now been abandoned as a result of the $1.5 billion cut in development assistance. The Government says that maybe we will get to 0.6 per cent by 1995. We say that is not good enough. It is completely inappropriate in terms of the role that Canada plays in the international community, completely inappropriate.
My colleagues will have much more to say about our concerns with the Budget in the specific areas they represent as spokespersons for our Party.
I move, seconded by the Hon. Member for Kenora-Rainy River (Mr. Parry):
That the amendment be amended by changing the period at the end of the last sentence to a comma and by adding immediately thereafter the following words: "and this House further condemns the Government for its brutal, uncaring and unfair tax increases on average income families while at the same time lowering taxes for upper income families and the corporate sector, and for its refusal to undertake an overhaul of the income tax system to bring about tax fairness and to give Canadians a tax system that they can understand."

Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on his very fine challenge to the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) and the Government in putting forward the impact this Budget will have on Canadians.
Has the Hon. Member any views on the Budget's impact on women? I did not see anything that mentioned equality for women. Women are already far behind in the workforce. We have cuts in employment training programs which will have a disproportionate effect on women. There is absolutely nothing in the Budget that refers to child care. There is a desperate need for action in this area within the next year. There are cut-backs in health and welfare programs which will have a dramatic disproportionate effect on women as well as cuts in transfer payments. The Minister, supposedly responsible for women in a crummy kind of advocate because he did not have a thing included in the Budget applying to women in a positive way. The Minister was at the Nairobi conference. He is sitting there. He has allowed development programs which are desperately needed by women and children around the world to be cut back. This Budget is hurting women in Canada and women around the world. I know my hon. friend has comments to make on that.

That is why I said at the outset that it is a very uncaring and callous Budget. It indicates a Government that does not care about the people of Canada. Perhaps it does not understand Canadians and the economic and social suffering that is going on.
In response to my hon. colleague, in all of the Budget documents there is virtually nothing that addresses the plight faced by women in Canada.

Is the New Democratic Party opposed, as I understand it, to the rural transition program? The Hon. Member had nothing but criticism toward that program. I will be surprised if that is

true because the Member was supporting the Canadian Job Strategy Program which discriminates against farmers and does not permit farmers to participate in it. subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: I will keep my question short and say more on the Budget later. speakeroldname: Hon. Michel Cote (Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs and Canada Post):
speakerposition: Minister responsible for Canada Post Corporation; Minister of Consumer and Corporate Affairs
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 consider it an honour to speak in the House today on the important legislation tabled yesterday, and I am referring to the Budget of my hon. colleague the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson).
Mr. Speaker, you will remember that during the last election campaign, our party was in favour of returning to sound management principles in public administration, a change that was absolutely essential because of the incredible growth of the federal deficit up to that time. When a country the size of ours gets to the point where it has a national debt of $200 billion, it is hardly exaggerating to talk about a disaster situation. Now I am sorry for the Members opposite, but they are mainly responsible for this state of affairs.
Mr. Speaker, to support my claim need I mention that for the current financial year, servicing the public debt alone will cost the incredible sum of nearly $26 billion? This is more than a thousand times the population of Canada. In a veritable frenzy of spending, the previous administration ended up spending the equivalent of 26 per cent of our Gross National Product. When a Government manages to spend more than one-quarter of what the country produces, I think that alone should be enough to muzzle our hon. friends opposite or at least make them blush with shame.
The result of more than twenty years of Liberal government boils down to this: During that period, the cumulative debt rose from $17 to $223 billion. This means it became fourteen times as big, and in 1985, it added up to $22,000 per Canadian family. Today, every Canadian family of four has to spend
The Budget-Hon. M. Cote
more than $4,200 per year on interest payments alone on the national debt. This means that every week, that same family has to spend more than $80 on this item. It means that every day, nearly $12 per family goes to repaying the interest on the profiligate spending of our hon. friends opposite. The situation became untenable, and Canadians gave us a mandate to put the country back on the road to common sense. Consequently, we opted for the implementation of three specific principles. First, restoring fiscal responsibility; second, increasing the effectiveness of public management, and third, providing maximum encouragement for private initiative.
As my hon. colleague the Minister of Finance pointed out yesterday, we have applied these principles very strictly, and we are already getting concrete results. The national debt is regressing, and will certainly continue to do so. The objective of our administration is still to eliminate wasteful expenditures and streamline Government operations. When someone is up to his neck in debt, common sense dictates belt tightening and, if at all possible, selling certain assets to accelerate repayments. That, Mr. Speaker, is exactly what we are doing.
One of our first moves in the fall of 1984 was to set up the Ministerial Task Force on Program Review responsible for recommending specific measures to reduce administrative overlapping, rationalize operations and, we believe, make significant savings. As the Minister of Finance pointed out, the detailed findings of the task force will be made public on March 11. In the current fiscal year this initiative has already made it possible to save more than $530 million. With that in mind, Mr. Speaker, we have decided to privatize certain Crown corporations. The Government has already sold most of its assets in the Canada Development Corporation, as it did in the case of the Northern Transportation Company and de Havilland. A number of other Crown corporations will also be sold to private interests in the coming months.
With a view to recouping a larger share of costs to service users, the Government of Canada has revised its rate schedules for various goods and services such as fares on federal ferry boats and inspection fees. For instance, Mr. Speaker, at the Department of Consumer and Corporate Affairs, we have substantially increased the charges for our metrological inspections.
One of the most important aspects of this program of cost recovery for services provided certainly involves the Canada Post Corporation. As underlined by my colleague, the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), the Canada Post Corporation has made substantial efforts in the last few years to reduce its costs and increase its productivity. We have only to recall, for instance, Mr. Speaker, that in 1985-86, its operating losses amounted to approximately $347 million while they will be approximately $243 million this year.
However, Mr. Speaker, these efforts are not enough to meet our objective of increasing the efficiency of the Government machine, and especially the Canada Post Corporation. I have

therefore asked the Chairman of the Corporation to submit to me as soon as possible a new operational plan providing for elimination of the operational deficit of the Canada Post Corporation by the end of the 1987-88 fiscal year, as requested by the Minister of Finance.
Obviously, the objective of a better postal service for Canadians remains an absolute priority, even in this context of financial self-sufficiency. Indeed, I shall have other opportunities is to come back to this issue in the coming weeks.
Beyond past and future savings, however, the budget brought down yesterday by the Minister of Finance proposes to keep at the same level as last year expenditures for statutory programs, which will represent in real terms a 4 per cent reduction.
Not only will the cost of these programs be limited to the level of last year, but, within its comprehensive cost reduction and public management improvement strategy, the Government will also apply a 2 per cent general reduction of all departmental budgets. This reduction will represent savings of over $500 million and will affect expenditures such as those related to capital costs, operations and maintenance, travel, advertising, and so on. Whole programs have been eliminated in this effort to provide stricter management of Government activities.
Here are just a few, Mr. Speaker, the Canadian Home Insulation Program, the Petroleum Incentives Program, the Petroleum Compensation Program, the Katimavik Program, the VIA Rail subsidies and, finally, the heavy water plants in Cape Breton.
Needless to say that it would be impossible to improve the productivity of the Government administration without controlling the Public Service. As we have already announced, the authorized number of person-years will be reduced by 2 percent next year, and another percent in each of the next four years, so that by 1990 the Public Service will have decreased by 15,000 person-years.
Together, Mr. Speaker, these various measures will mean a reduction of $6 billion in Government spending as compared to what was originally forecasted. For the whole period from 1986 to 1990-91, these measures will represent savings of nearly $80 billion.

The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) also announced a number of new measures aimed at assisting low-income Canadians. First, he talked about the Child Tax Credit. Members will recall that the May, 1985 Budget provided for an increase in the Child Tax Credit to $384 per child in the taxation year. We are not, however, stopping here. The Child
Tax Credit will be further increased to $454 per child in 1986 to $489 in 1987, and to $524 in the 1988 taxation year.
As part of the efforts of this Government to ensure that the federal benefits program reach those directly in need, and to do away with the negative social impact of the tax rebate discount, and as I have announced it during the debate on amendment of the Tax Rebating Discounting Act, a system of advance or prepayment of the Child Tax Credit will be introduced for 1986 and subsequent years. As announced by the Minister of Finance this prepayment will amount to $300 per child, or about two-thirds of the maximum payment for recipients who had family incomes of $15,000 or less in 1985. Claimants will receive this payment automatically in November, 1986, rather than be forced to wait until the filing of their tax return in early 1987. Since this prepayment will be based on 1985 tax returns there will be no additional administrative burden imposed upon claimants. This will benefit about one million Canadian families.
Too often low-income Canadians, and expecially Child Tax Credit recipients, have been encouraged to use discounting services because they did not have their rightful benefit in hand at the moment they needed it. This system of prepayments will ensure that this money goes directly to those who need it most, rather than going to tax discounters.
Second, the Government is introducing a new refundable sales tax credit of $50 per adult and $25 per child for families whose income is below $15,000. More than four million Canadian families will receive this credit. This is clearly a fundamental innovation to the income tax system that will resolve in significant benefits to low-income Canadians, many of whom are elderly.
Third, the disability deduction available to 185,000 disabled Canadians will be increased by $250 in 1986. The total deduction will now be worth $2,860 for 1986.
Fourth, a special training program for Canadians or social assistance will be established. The federal Government will commit up to $100 million per year for the next three years. Matching funds will be provided also by provincial Governments. This new program will help train Canadians on welfare, enabling them to find meaningful employment. The Government's commitment to social justice is clear and ongoing. Yesterday's Budget continues this effort.

subtopic: TRIBUTE TO HON. JEAN CHRETIEN, FORMER MEMBER FOR SAINT-MAURICE

Mr. Speaker, 1 want to say a few words about a former Member of Parliament. I refer to Jean Chretien, the former Hon. Member for Saint-Maurice. I was unable to make such remarks this morning, so I would like to join with the leaders of other Parties in saying a few words now.

Today, Jean Chretien may be leaving the political scene, but certainly not the Canadian scene. I am sure he will continue to influence the Canadian society in his inimitable fashion.
In all the portfolios he has held, whether that of Justice, Indian Affairs and Northern Development, Finance, National Revenue, or Energy, Mines and Resources, Jean Chretien demonstrated the same serious commitment. Obviously, I was not always in agreement with him. But nobody could doubt his impassioned dedication. He was both true Quebecer and a true Canadian.
I wish him the best of luck in the future.

Mr. Speaker, judging by the sterile comments voiced by the Opposition until now, one will realize that they have nothing to say. This would explain the level of their criticism which is inconsistent, unfounded, and worthless. They are truly disarmed, Mr. Speaker.
Under the Liberals, we were saddled with huge tax increases while the inflation rate was kept above the 12 per cent level, and that led to disastrous losses for the Canadian taxpayers.
The assumption is that the additional measures which Canadians will have to live with in order to make up for past wastefulness provide greater fairness and justice to citizens generally than under the previous Government. That, Mr. Speaker, is sound management, and we will carry on with the mandate entrusted by the people and with our role as trustees for the welfare and to the benefit of all groups in our society.

Mr. Speaker, February 26, 1986, will be seen as a historical and happy day for all Canadians because they had a chance yesterday to see that this Government's financial commitments have been upheld not a single one of our forecasts was overrun.
The actual deficit for 1985-86 will be $33.8 billion-our forecast was for a $33.8 billion deficit.
Our expenditures will not even reach the estimated level of $105 billion. For the first time in decades, there has been a reduction in absolute terms in program expenditures.
As against what the Opposition is suggesting, reducing our expenditures and the deficit will benefit the average Canadian, because he would have had to foot the bill had we not made such cuts.

Mr. Speaker, yesterday Parliament and the nation were presented with a gift. With the policies outlined by the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) we shall be able to pass on to our children and grandchildren the gift of a nation restored to financial health.
There is no greater gift than that of a future, and a future is just what the Government has offered Canadians. Gone are the days of "fly now and pay later". The Government has brought financial sanity back to our nation and thrown aside the irresponsible policies of spend, spend, spend.
Yes, the Government has presented the nation, in an open and forthright manner, with a game plan for economic renewal. It has plotted the course and it has led the way. History will commend the Minister of Finance for this Budget. Future generations will thank the Government for this precious gift that has been given to them.

February 27, 1986
Oral Questions EMPLOYMENT CRITICISM OF BUDGET MEASURES

Mr. Speaker, we have seen with this Budget that the Conservative Party has no heart for the old or for the young. Not only has the Government cut almost $30 million from the Labour Adjustment Program but it has refused, despite repeated pleas from all sides of the House, to bring back some kind of fairness to the unemployment insurance scheme.
The Government has cut off older workers. It has cut off younger workers. One in six young people in Canada today is without a job, and yet there was not one single word in the Budget about a whole lost generation. What we saw were cuts in the employment programs for young people, cuts of $100 million in the last Budget and $100 million in this Budget. There were cuts for the older workers, but at the same time the Government has enough money in its pocket to give tax rebates to the corporations. That is the true face of the Conservative Party. The old, the young, and the middle-class do not have a place in the "Big Blue Machine".

If we look at the figures in the Budget, we will see that the impact of the massive taxation falls on individuals and does not fall on corporations and businesses. As a matter of fact, over the next three years, corporate taxes will decline and taxes on individuals will increase.
I simply referred just a moment ago to the increases in taxes as a result of last night's Budget, but if those are put together with the increases in taxes imposed by the Budget of last May, the total increase in taxes for 1986-87, the next fiscal year, will be $6.2 billion, by 1990-91, it will be $13 billion, $13 billion taken out of the pockets of Canadians through taxation as a result of the two Budgets presented since the Conservatives came to power.
These are massive increases in taxation for individuals. Some say that they are the greatest increases in I 5 years. The tax reductions are for the benefit of corporations and very little is done for individuals.
As well, I must remind the House that the measures introduced in the Budget of May 1985 are still in effect. There is



February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Allmand
still a Bill going through Parliament designed to reduce the indexation on family allowances. That Bill is presently in the Senate. It was pushed through this House by means of closure. There is still legislation that provides for the deindexation of personal taxation and cut-backs on unemployment insurance for Canadians taking early retirement. The Government is not only massively raising taxes but also cutting back on Government programs and in many cases on Government programs which are useful to needy Canadians.
For example, as was referred to during Question Period by my colleague, the Hon. Member for Cape Breton-East Richmond (Mr. Dingwall), there has been a cut of $9.1 billion from the economic and regional development envelope, a cut amounting to 38 per cent over three years, a cut which will affect very severely the regions with very high unemployment which are facing difficult economic times. There are not only increases in taxation but very important and callous expenditure cuts. It is amazing that the Conservative Party bragged about those cuts as if it were a great achievement to take away benefits needed by Canadians to meet their daily needs of life.
The Canadian Jobs Strategy Program is being cut back by $100 million in 1987-88. There are employment programs in the Budget for older workers and welfare recipients, but those programs are vague for the time being and are being delayed. The Budget indicates that they will have to be worked out in due course with the provinces and the private sector. We do not really know the details of those programs, and in any case they do not come into effect right away. On the other hand, the taxes announced last night are certain and immediate. They come into effect as soon as possible.
With respect to the cuts, the blue book of Estimates which we just received today will reveal more. We will know what other spending programs will be cut back. However, the cutting of these programs, many of which had a humanitarian purpose, is nothing of which to be proud. Many of these programs provided essential services to needy Canadians and now those Canadians will have to do without those services and they will get to know about that as they begin to live with the situation of those programs no longer existing.
It is also clear that the cutting of the regional development programs and so on will lead to a situation where the gulf between the rich and the poor will become greater, where the rich will become richer and the poor will become poorer. A recent article in The Toronto Star indicated that welfare cases in Metropolitan Toronto were up by 48 per cent. It indicated that the number of people on general welfare in Metropolitan Toronto went up 48 per cent in the last four years, at a time when the Government was claiming that there had been a decline in unemployment. In fact, the number of working poor is increasing at a time when those people in the upper or richer brackets are becoming even richer and are escaping many of the tax measures that are being imposed upon those who earn income from salaries and wages. One could argue that not only are these measures to cut back on Government programs and to
impose heavy taxes on salaried and wage-earning Canadians cruel in themselves, but they are against the provisions of the new Constitution. Section 36 of the Constitution, one of the outstanding sections, is a very concise declaration of Liberal policy and philosophy. It indicates that without altering the legislative authority of Parliament or the provincial legislatures, or the rights of any of them in respect of the exercise of their legislative authority, Parliament and the legislatures, together with the Government of Canada, are committed to promoting equal opportunities for the well-being of Canada, furthering economic development to reduce disparity and opportunity, and providing essential public services of reasonable quality to all Canadians. We have a commitment in the Constitution by the Governments of Canada to narrow the gulf between the rich and the poor, not only on an individual basis, but on a regional basis-central Canada vis-a-vis the Atlantic area, the south of our country vis-a-vis the north of our country. There is a commitment in the Constitution to do that. The Government is cutting programs without paying any real attention to whether or not the programs are necessary. That is how it is being done. Priority has not been given to the programs themselves but simply to cutting back.
This imposition of taxes is contrary, if not to the letter of Article 36 of the Constitution, at least to the spirit of it. The gulf is getting larger all the time, yet the Government persists with a program which it believes will bring good to the country. The Government's models in all this are Margaret Thatcher in Great Britain and Ronald Reagan in the United States. It is interesting to read an editorial which appeared in the New York International Herald Tribune and was written in London, England. It dealt with the growing criticism against the Thatcher Government for doing the very thing which our Government is doing in the Budget. It read in part:
Mrs. Thatcher's rivals from the libera! wing of the Conservative Party now say to her that enough is enough, and that the unemployed should be put to work to build needed housing and public works. They say that industry should be backed by government, just as it is in France, West Germany, and Japan; that "not everything can be left to market forces"-
The critics are calling for a restoration of that measure of social spending and of government intervention in the economy that is both traditional Conservative Party policy and exists in one form or another in all Western European countries.
It is true that it has been a tradition of Conservative Parties, of Liberal Parties and of Social Democratic Parties to try to bring back some balance between the rich and the poor. Since the Second World War, Governments in western democracies have played the role of redistributing wealth in their countries. It has only been in the last few years, under the Governments of Reagan in the United States and of Thatcher in England, that there has been an abandonment of that principle of Government. As was pointed out in the editorial, it was even a policy of Conservative Parties at one time. The tide is turning in Britain. They have seen the result of that type of policy-a widened gulf between the rich and the poor, and a two-tiered society in which there is turmoil and in which there are soccer and race riots in the great northern cities of Britain because not enough attention is being paid to the humanitarian side, to social problems or to political problems. The total concentra-
February 27, 1986

tion has been on the bottom line, on what is profitable and on what is and is not a deficit. That is not enough in the long run. As a matter of fact it is even poor economic policy because these conditions undermine economic well-being.
At the present time there are 4.5 million people living below the poverty line in Canada. There were several measures in the Budget of last May and the one of last night which are contrary to long-standing traditions in western democracies of dealing with broad-based social and economic problems. The Government, with these two Budgets, is abandoning its traditional role of equalizer between the rich and the poor to ensure that the wealth of the country is distributed more fairly.
Let me concentrate for a few minutes on the problem of unemployment. It was very interesting during Question Period today when I asked questions of the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). It was mentioned in the Budget that they expected to have a 9 per cent unemployment rate at the end of 1987, which is a full three years after the turn around in the recession. The recession not only hit Canada; it hit the whole western world. A full three years later the Minister is still willing to accept a 9 per cent unemployment rate. In a supplementary answer he said that he did not accept it, but there was no other target in the Budget. The only target mentioned in that document was the 9 per cent. I pointed out to him that in 1981, the year before the recession, the average rate of unemployment in Canada was 7.5 per cent. In the period from 1965 to 1980, it was 5.6 per cent. It jumped in one year, from 1981 to 1982, to 11.9 per cent.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Who was in Government?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The Liberals were in government. The Conservatives were in Government in Britain under the same circumstances, and it jumped to 13 per cent and is still 13 per cent. The Government ignores the fact that the recession is over and it is still willing to live with a rate of unemployment which is much higher than it was in pre-recession times. It is putting its head in the sand and is ignoring the feelings of the people of the country. When we read the editorials and the polls on this subject, it is evident that the Canadian public is not impressed with the repeated claims about the 580,000 jobs. Perhaps it is because there are so many new Members in the House that many of them do not know anything about what happened before September, 1984. The Conservatives boast that these 580,000 jobs in 17 months, from September, 1984 to January, 1986, is some kind of a record. That is false. In the 17 month-period from August, 1978 to January, 1980, 597,000 new jobs were created, and 631,000 new jobs were created in the 17-month period from September, 1972 to January, 1974 in a smaller labour market.

speakerposition: Minister of Labour; Minister responsible for Canada Mortgage and Housing Corporation
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: What recession are you talking about?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
That was a period of expansion, and it should be a period of expansion right now. Here we have a Government in a post-recession period yet willing to live with a 9 per cent unemployment rate and doing nothing about it. As a matter of fact there are only two measures in the Budget that
The Budget-Mr. Allmand
will do anything very specific about unemployment. One has to deal with older workers and that for the moment is very vague. The program will not come into efect until God knows when, for many months, if not years, because there is no target. The Government says it has to be developed with the provinces and with the private sector. There is also a program to help find employment for people on welfare, but that also is vague. It has to be negotiated and is sometime in the future.
Ministers get up one after the other and boast about their great performance. But what is the reaction of the Canadian public? Another Gallup poll published today showed that over 55 per cent of Canadians have little faith in the Government's jobless tactics. In a poll published on January 13, 1986, 50 per cent say that unemployment is still the major concern.
The editorial I read into the record the other day came from the St. John's evening Telegram for February 8, 1986. Its headline read, "Nothing to Cheer about when there are still 1.25 Million Canadians Unemployed Three Years after the Recession and we have a Government that is still Happy with its Record in Employment". I have an editorial that expresses the situation very well. It is from The New York Times on the situation in the United States where the unemployment rate is down to 6.6 per cent. It reads, in part:
Still, Too Few Have Jobs.
Each month the White House trumpets another increase in the number of Americans with jobs.-Even 6.6 per cent is high unemployment, especially so in a strong economy.-For unemployment to endure at such high levels is bad news.
The same thing applies in Canada, Mr. Speaker. This Budget is a massive gouging of Canadian taxpayers and consumers through taxation and cuts in Government programs. It is a Budget which, I believe, will not stimulate prosperity but will retard the recovery because it is taking too much out of the economy at a time when we want to expand. It is a Budget which has given no priority whatever to unemployment. There is nothing for youth unemployment, nothing for those who are on long-term unemployment, and nothing for women. It is a Budget that is a very regressive economic document that has very little to say about it in micro or macro economic terms. I believe that once Canadians have had an opportunity to read it and to feel its impact, the standing of the Government will fall even faster than it did after the last Budget.
By repeating misleading figures over and over, as the old saying goes, you can fool some of the people some of the time but a lot of them are going to find out sooner or later what the real situation is. Then you will face the reality of the anger and frustration of those Canadians who are not getting a fair deal and cannot Find the jobs they deserve.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Are there any questions or comments? Debate. The Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Nipigon.

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Epp (Thunder Bay-Nipigon)

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have under the Standing Orders of the House 20 minutes to address the subject this afternoon. I regret that because there is a great deal to be said on this Budget. The people of Canada and my constituents in Thunder Bay-Nipigon certainly expect us to speak to the Budget and to express their indignation and outrage at what the Government plans to do to them.
There are only 70 of us in the Opposition, and since this morning only 69. I would think Canadians from coast to coast would wish that there were many more of us in the Opposition to speak honestly to the situation facing us and make quite clear how much the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has misjudged his targets in deciding how to deal with economic situations and what kinds of taxes and spending plans to arrive at.
Last night at eleven o'clock I had a call from a constituent. I was busy looking through some of the pre-Budget speculation in the press. He wanted to underscore his reaction against the Budget, against the taxing proposals it included, and to encourage me to be very clear about his reaction and the reaction of many people in Thunder Bay-Nipigon at what the Government presumes to do.
1 assured him that I would have the opportunity this afternoon and, given the Budget which the Government has laid on us, I appreciate the opportunity to say something about its shortcomings.
I think it is worth taking a moment to consider our situation. The Minister of Finance has done that from his own limited perspectives. Of course, the Government has done a good deal to emphasize the good things that happened in 1985. 1 think we can say that the Government and the Canadian people were lucky in 1985. Interest rates fell. The existence of a new Government gave many people hope. As a result of those factors, a good deal of them coming from outside the country, things improved.
I remember being shocked about a year ago to have a Conservative back-bencher tell me that the Government's budget plans were tied into hopes that Canada would be able to ride toward recovery on the coat-tails of the Americans. If we could only tie into the American recovery, we would be in luck. In 1985, we got a certain measure of that luck but there is no assurance in 1986 that we will get the same thing. There is every possibility that interest rates will not decline. Certainly real interest rates, the difference between the inflation rate and the going interest rates, are very, very high. There is concern about what will happen to the dollar.
Actions of the Government, particularly focusing on deficits have done a good deal to bring uncertainty into the money markets. The stupid statement of the Prime Minister (Mr. Mulroney) last September, for example, that Canada was bankrupt was one of those irresponsible statements that would sooner or later come home to roost. Unfortunately, when it does, it does so for all Canadians.
The uncertainty in the energy markets is surely designed to make 1986 as perilous a year on an international basis as well
as in Canada as we have had for a long time. All of that brings into question the proposition of the Minister of Finance that we will have a 3.7 per cent growth rate in Canada. If we are that lucky, we will see a decline in unemployment of 0.2 per cent which, given a growing labour force, could mean no decline at all in the number of people who are unemployed.
That is the situation that we face in 1986. What could the Government have done about these circumstances? What would have ensured that this would be a Budget for prosperity rather than a prescription for continued depression in the outlying regions of the country and depression in southern Ontario where the recovery of 1985 was the most obvious? What is there to ensure that my constituents in Thunder Bay-Nipigon, who have been very responsive to the arguments that the country desperately needs tax reform, will do better, that they will live better and that more business will be done in the shops and the stores in Thunder Bay if there is an improvement in the fairness and a decline in the unfairness of the present tax system? What hope do we have out of the Budget given to us yesterday afternoon?
I do not think there is any hope at all in those terms. One of the uncertain factors for 1986 is the increasing weight of taxation on individual Canadians and on families. The increasing weight of taxation includes particularly very sharp increases in sales taxes which are borne by all Canadians. The Government has been half-way compassionate enough to recognize that sales taxes bear heavily on everyone, no matter what their income level, and so there is a refund of some of the sales tax in this credit proposal, which is one of the two bright spots in the Budget. The other is some small changes in tax expenditures. In that we see recognition of how serious the effect of the Budget will be on people all across the country.
The weight of taxation is a fundamental problem which faces the Canadian economy. I want to say something about that while emphasizing that the Government's need for revenue, which is obvious to everyone, is the challenge which the Minister of Finance chose to address, but in a most misguided way. If we needed revenue, why, in God's name and in the name of Canadian prosperity, did the Minister of Finance not consider that great range of tax breaks, which he knows is out there, which he has tried to estimate but many of which he has been unable to estimate?
Why did he not come to grips with more than the inventory credit and the investment tax credit provisions which, between them, are expected to bring in $380 million while the 3 per cent surtax on personal income tax alone is expected to bring in $560 million? That is a measure of how half-hearted, tentative, and almost nonexistent the response of the Minister of Finance is to the enormous revenue challenges that face him and to the incredible unfairness of the Canadian tax system.
There is a need for revenue. Why was there not a consideration of the other tax expenditures? There was no shortage of discussion of them. Speculation in the press focused on these. 1 could point out various instances to which others pointed.
February 27, 1986

Some of them, of course, would bear on individuals. Far more of them would bear on the activities of corporations. As John Bulloch, President of the Canadian Federation of Independent Business, recognizes so well, the areas that encourage large companies to spend money on capital equipment should be dealt with, because they are designed to reduce employment. When economic activity is slow there is no investment of this sort taking place anyway. Therefore, to provide breaks to companies is a short-sighted thing to do.
The Minister of Finance blew the opportunities in these areas. I would like to put two of them together in a way which may perhaps be somewhat novel. Lottery earnings are not taxable in this country. It is estimated that if lottery prizes were taxed it might produce $500 million to $600 million for the Government. It is possible that it would bring in even more money than the 3 per cent surtax on personal incomes does now. There was no such proposal.
However, insurance awards remain taxable. When making decisions on liability insurance claims judges will have to make adjustments for tax losses in order to ensure that someone who has won a suit resulting from an injury receives a decent income. Judges will have to drive the amounts up into the billion dollar range. Surely one could have considered making insurance awards of this sort, which are rare enough in this country, nontaxable, while at the same time taxing lottery prizes where blind luck is involved. In the process every Canadian would have benefited. It may have been possible to avoid a 3 per cent surtax on personal incomes, and it would surely have been possible to introduce some stability into the insurance market which has been incredibly difficult over the last weeks. There is an example of some novel thinking which should have been brought to bear in drafting this Budget. There was nothing of the sort, of course.
This Budget is a continuation of the principles of budgetmaking which go back to the early 1970s. This is in fact a Lib-Con Budget. It is the kind of Budget that Liberal Finance Ministers have brought forward quite a number of times, including the restraint. It is perhaps more severe on the taxation side. My Conservative colleagues would surely throw the petroleum and gas revenue tax at me as an instance of a similar kind of Liberal Budget, just to underscore the point that there is not much to choose from between Liberals and Conservatives when they are Ministers of Finance.
What is the consequence of the taxation systems that we have had over the past 13 or 14 years? One of the consequences which the Minister of Finance is obsessed by is a national debt that is nearing $225 billion. If the Auditor General is right that the tax expenditures are running at anywhere from $30 billion to $50 billion a year now, the larger part of that being to the advantage of corporate enterprise, then the Canadian people bear a national debt burden of over $200 billion, which matches the amount of money that has been put into the pockets of large corporations, managers, shareholders, and so on, over the last dozen years.
What is the consequence of that? In the current budget year the Government is hoping for budgetary revenue of over $70
The Budget-Mr. Epp (Thunder Bay-Nipigort) billion. Of that, $37 billion will come from personal income tax. If the interest on the national debt next year is $27 billion, then three-quarters of what all Canadians pay in taxes will go toward interest on the national debt. If successive Liberal and Conservative Governments have financed corporate enterprise with our money to the tune of $225 billion, and that represents an interest loan next year of $27 billion, then three-quarters of the money that all of us will be paying to the Government of Canada is going to go to those who hold the Government's financial instruments. We are going to be loaded down with more and more tax and are going to be paying more and more of our hard-earned money to the Government of Canada for transfer to those who have had the money over the last dozen years to buy the Government's financial instruments.
That is what Lib-Con Budgets have done. The Canadian people have been conned in the most incredible way. Big enterprises in the country have been enriched in the most astounding way. All of us, as individuals, pay the shot to the financial institutions that hold such large portions of these instruments. If they are not financial institutions, they are surely prosperous Canadians who have the money to invest in these. They get some of it back if they pay taxes and also hold these. That is the result of a dozen years or more of budgeting.
Did we see any recognition of that on the part of the Minister of Finance? Did we see any recognition that this country is in desperate need of real tax reform in which the tax expenditures are dealt with? All of those that do not generate employment in this country are done away with so that the mind, and spirit-sapping impact of unemployment would be ended for the Canadian people. Did we see any of that? No, we did not. We saw our Minister of Finance remain obsessed with a national debt, whose total he does not consider in terms of how it was built up and who is quite prepared to continue to burden individual Canadians with this kind of taxation. On these facts ordinary Canadians are not going to support the Conservative Party. If I had my way they would not allow Liberals to con them into thinking that the Liberal Party will do any better, because its record over the years is responsible for much of this.
The Minister of Finance has done his part to add to the complexity of a tax system that everyone knows is almost incomprehensible. I had a Government back-bencher telling me just yesterday after the Budget Speech that my colleague, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), is absolutely on the right track, maybe not so much on fairness as on simplifying the tax system. The Minister of Finance does not plan to do that.
Colleagues from the Conservative Party, do you really expect the people of Canada to support you when you pull off that kind of stunt? There is a tax revolt building in this country. I discovered in the election campaign of 1984 that that is a tax revolt that we New Democrats can lead. 1 am going to do my part to see to it that the people of Canada know exactly how you, as well as the Liberals, are transferring

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Epp (Thunder Bay-Nipigon) their hard-earned money into the wealth of those who control the large enterprises, the seven families and groups that dominate so much of our economy. I want them to know that that is what Liberals and Conservatives do to them. Once they appreciate those things, there is going to be a political revolution in this country that will surprise you and be enormously gratifying to me and to my constituents in Thunder Bay-Nipi-gon who desperately want to lead good and prosperous lives to find the employment that the Government promised them. The Conservatives are not going to do that. In fact, the Minister of Finance has suggested that he wants to get the balance of program expenditures back to the early 1960s. He is too much of an economist and has been absent from here so that he does not remember what the early 1960s were. A lot of Canadians have not forgotten the Diefenbaker depression. If he wants to take us back to that time, the only good thought I can utter is that he might try to take us back to the more balanced tax situation of those days, a good deal closer to fairness between the corporate and the individual. For the 1.3 million Canadians who continue to look for work and are told by the Minister of Finance that if the growth rate is really terrific this year at 3.7 per cent we may see a 0.2 per cent decline in unemployment, this could mean, as happened in January when it dropped to under 10 per cent, that there were actually more people looking for work in January than there had been before because the labour force continues to grow.
The Canadian people expected a lot better. The Minister of Finance, when he was in the Opposition, spoke at various places against the Finance Minister of the time, Allan Mac-Eachen. I have a copy of his speech to the Canadian Club here. He quoted a businessman at the time saying to him, "What could the Government do for the value of the dollar?" He hesitated for a moment and then said, "Mr. MacEachen could rise from his seat in the House and say, 'I quit'." I think that that is a fair thing to say to a Minister of Finance who has been an incredibly naive man and politically insensitive. If Michael Wilson would like to rise in his place in the House and say, "I quit" then the country would stand a better chance of becoming the prosperous place that my constituents and people from coast to coast want it to be.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I have just a comment and three points I would like my hon. friend to respond to. He was attacking the sale tax increase and, in fairness, he did acknowledge that there was the sale tax credit, which will help lower income Canadians, and I thank him for that acknowledgement. He went on to make quite an attack on the corporate tax system. I would like his comment on this, because a corporation is nothing more than a legal fiction. Any taxes imposed on that corporation are simply passed through on the price of their goods to the consumers. To increase the corporate tax has always seemed to me personally to be a regressive tax very much like the sales tax. If a corporation is building widgets it is going to pass that through, because if it does not pass it through it is going to go out of business.
There is quite a strong argument that corporate taxes should be seen in the same light as sales taxes as compared to the
progressive income tax that is levied on people so that the people with more wealth pay more than those with less wealth. I would like his comment on that.
With respect to lotteries, it has long been thought that if you make an investment for a business you deduct the cost of interest on the money against the earnings. If we are going to tax the earnings of lotteries then surely the Government would have to permit a deduction of the tickets purchased, which leads you to the position that if you sell 14 million tickets at $1 and $14 million are deducted from income tax, in order for somebody to win $5 million-because the rest of that money, the difference between the pay-out and the number of tickets sold, goes usually into charitable goods-will we not be in a net loss position? I would appreciate his comment on that.
The last point is with respect to tax expenditures. I wonder if he would be kind enough to acknowledge that it was the present Minister of Finance who, in 1984, for the first time since the former Conservative Minister of Finance in 1979, filed a statement listing all the tax expenditures? So that it has really been only a year since we have had a general public debate to find out how large those expenditures are in terms of our personal deductions, our spousal deductions, our child deductions, and, true, all of the benefits that go through to corporations. Surely as part of that national debate he would recognize that one year is not an unduly long time. The Minister has already attacked about nine of those tax expenditures, and I am sure we can expect more in the future. Will he acknowledge that that was a wise policy move to publish that document?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
I thank my colleague for those questions. As far as the taxation of corporations is concerned, I know there has been a prevailing tendency for some time to argue the proposition that he suggests, that corporations should not be taxed; we should just tax the ultimate recipients of the gains, if you will. The fact of the matter is that you can talk about legal fictions or whatever, what counts in the courts is the existence of the corporation as a legal person. It does not take any perception at all, in examining corporations at work, to realize that they are, in fact, most active and constructive, dynamic, acquisitive, legal personalities. The Hon. Member refers to the fact that corporations use a good deal of this profit. Perhaps I should refer to the fact that in using these retained earnings for investment purposes corporations are doing some odd things, at least in economic theory. One would think that if there were anything like free competition prevailing then these profits would be competed away. What we see instead is corporations that have substantial retained earnings and are able to use them to invest. This fact leads me to think that having these legal persons in the country not by any means distributing anything like all of the earnings that they take in justifies our saying that if they are going to use them for investment purposes they should share some of those earnings with the people of Canada. This is in order to reduce the weight of taxation on individuals so that those individuals would have larger incomes which they could take off to supermarkets and shopping
February 27, 1986

centres to buy products these companies produce which would keep them in business. These people who make this particular argument for the corporation seem to forget completely that they are in the business of making money. The way to make money is to have business grow, and the only way to have business grow is to have people with more money to spend. That means sharing in the burden of taxation, so that that particular argument follows.
Perhaps in an analogous way 1 can suggest that 1 would not be in favour of giving people a credit for the purchase of lottery tickets. But when one makes this windfall gain, I think the people of Canada have a right to share in it in the same way the people of Canada expect to share in capital gains of all sorts, and they are mostly outraged at the $500,000 capital gains tax holiday which the Minister of Finance offered in the Budget of last spring.
As far as the tax expenditures to which the Flon. Member referred are concerned, if he will check I think he will find that it was in August, 1985 that the Minister published the statement on various tax expenditures. So it is even less in that sense than the time he suggested. The fact that the Minister did not use the opportunity in the February Budget to do anything more significant than a couple of measures which will bring in some $380 million when tax expenditures run from $30 billion to $50 billion, suggests to me that the Minister of Finance has blown an opportunity. He talked tough, but instead of being tough with the people with whom he should have been tough, that is, the corporations, he socked it to individual Canadians.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, 1 would like to comment on what was said by the Hon. Member for Thunder Bay-Atikokan (Mr. Angus). Mr. Speaker, I think it is a sad reflection on the Hon. Member that he is trying to frighten Canadians and predicting all kinds of gloom and doom for 1986. Unlike the Hon. Member, 1 think the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) brought down a very realistic and very responsible Budget yesterday evening. And why do we have a realistic Budget. Mr. Speaker? Because we also have to deal with what happened previously.
The cumulative deficit had reached $200 billion when we came to power on September 4, 1984, and if we had continued the previous Government's policies, twenty years from now the deficit would have been one trillion dollars, and for the taxpayer, $1 trillion with a 10 per cent interest rate would mean that twenty years from now, the cost of servicing the debt would be almost as high as the sum total of the Budget. Yesterday evening, being realistic meant realizing that we are in a difficult financial situation, and, Mr. Speaker, this is the first Minister of Finance in twenty years who has attained his objective. He told Canadians we had to bring down the deficit. And he talked about cutting $4 billion off the deficit. Well, we
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
went from 38.2 to 33.8 billion this year, which I think this is a vast improvement, and we are now talking about cutting another four billion off the deficit to bring it down to 29.2 billion. That is less than $30 billion, and I think that shows the Government's message is a serious one.
I also said this was a responsible Budget. Mr. Speaker, what is the most important source of jobs in this country? Small business. There are 700,000 small businesses in this country. The Government has great confidence in this sector, and that is why the tax rate on small business income will be reduced from 15 per cent to 13 per cent, to help small businesses generate new investment in the economy and create additional jobs. I believe that our performance in our first year is good enough to warrant the trust of Canadians. We created 580,000 jobs in fifteen months, more than in all sixteen European countries combined. I think that is a good performance. We must persevere and continue along the same path, and that was the message the Minister of Finance gave us yesterday.
I also think we considered another important aspect which is to help those Canadians who are most in need, and I am referring to two measures more specifically, including the $300 prepayment of the tax credit to families whose income is less than $15,000. Furthermore, in connection with the one per cent increase the sales tax, the Government will provide a refundable sales tax credit of $50 per adult and $25 per child, and I think that is important. We have considered the plight of the neediest and poorest in our society, and I think that is what responsible Government means. Mr. Speaker, I wish my hon. friend would remember this in his comments.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Would the Hon. Member care to reply?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Yes, Mr. Speaker. I will be very brief, as I should be. The Hon. Member makes the same kind of speech he and his colleagues will be making all over the country, I do not doubt. The situation is a very serious one and the Minister of Finance has focused wrongly in trying to come to grips with it. Rhetoric may work. But if this year turns out to be as difficult as anticipated, then the Canadian people will surely become all the more unhappy. It is a matter of how one sees these things, not a matter of piling up rhetoric to suggest how well things are going to turn out.

speakerposition: Deputy Chair of Committees of the Whole
subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: The period for questions and comments has now terminated. Debate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am deeply honoured to speak in this debate. Budget debates have been part of the parliamentary tradition since 1773 and none has had more importance in the parliamentary year than the budget debate. This is especially so in terms of this budget debate in Canada in the year 1986. There has been no debate in the history of this Parliament, and in the history of this country, more significant for our national future than the debate on our Budget and the policies it represents. These

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
policies are vital to Canada's future. Because of these policies the future can be worthy of our past.
A few weeks ago in the riding of Scarborough West, in one of our public schools, I spoke to a class. One of the children asked me what I would choose if I could choose anything 1 wanted the Government to do. I answered that I would teach Canadians to be proud of Canada. We have so much of which to be proud as a people. No twenty-five million people in the world have done what we have done as a people. We have a population equal to that of the State of California, yet we have taken the second largest country in the world, with one of the most challenging environments, and have made it into one of the major industrial countries in the world. We have such a distinguished history of which to be proud, yet so very few years ago that one would only need one hand to count them, Canadians were wondering if they had a future. They wondered if the future of their country would be in any way like the past of which they were so proud. The answer to their concerns, and the reason why Canadians are no longer worried about their future, is the success of the economic policies which have been put into place by the Government since its election in the fall of 1984.
This Budget is not to be considered on its own. It should be seen as part of an economic plan which began with the Economic Statement of November 1984. It was continued in the Budget in the spring of 1985 and has now taken a significant step further in the Budget of February, 1986.
I would like to review ways in which those economic policies have guaranteed to the people of Canada that we can anticipate a future which will be worthy of the past of which we are so proud. First, our policies have been aimed at reducing the deficit. This has been a major challenge. Indeed, it is a challenge which has concerned the world, which in turn has given its judgement on the Canadian dollar, and that was in large part because of the concern with the deficit, and with good reason. In the year 1975, the deficit represented $87 per capita. In the last year of the Liberal Government, it represented $1,469 per man, woman and child. That is the Liberal record. The Liberals themselves knew what was wrong. They talked reduction. They talked as if they believed they should reduce the deficit. The Minister of Finance in 1980, the Hon. Allan MacEachen, said in his budget address: "We must slow down the growth of public debt charges". Three years later, the Minister of Finance, the Hon. Marc Lalonde, made a stab at it when he said: "We must manage the deficit now to ensure it will come down as quickly as possible". Year after year the Liberal talked reduction, but we have done it. The Liberals had debt charges which in 1975 represented $3,025,000,000. That was the total charges for servicing the public debt in 1975. By the end of the Liberals' term in office, those charges had risen to $22,500,000,000. No wonder people are worried about this country having a future on which they can rely. It is no wonder people are concerned that their country, which was so affluent, prosperous and strong is going down the pipe. They can now be assured that the future is something in which they can have confidence, for, at last, reducing the deficit is
not something about which a Government talks but something about which a Government does.
Second, our policies as a Government have been aimed at restraining Government expenditures. That is also something in which our Liberal predecessors believed. The present Leader of the Opposition (Mr. Turner), when he was Minister of Finance in 1975, said that no measure is more important than the control of public expenditures. It was with good reason that he said that, for public expenditures had escalated beyond belief. At the most intensive time of World War II, public expenditures by the Government of Canada totalled $5.5 billion. A generation later, in 1967-68, they had doubled to about $11 billion. And what are they now? I wish it were possible to say that we are reducing expenditures to such an extent that we are getting back to those days when they represented a much smaller part of the Gross National Product. However, we must take heart when we consider that the Estimates submitted by the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) this very day show that we have almost zero growth in the expenditures of the country for the second year in a row, while other costs in our society are growing steadily. There is still growth with respect to the cost of living to the tune of 4 per cent. But the cost of Government is not keeping pace with that. Why would the country not have renewed confidence in the future when it sees that at last through its Government its people are gaining some control on Government spending?
Third, our policies stand for reshaping Government and reducing deficits. We are restraining expenditures and reshaping Government. As the Minister of Finance said in his impressive address last night, we need not more Government, we need more effective Government. I draw to the attention of Members of the House and to the attention of the public three specific ways in which we can do this. For example, the Government is introducing a merit criterion for increasing the salaries of executives. That is a new thought. When did this country's civil service ever have itself challenged by the prospect of showing merit as the standard for gaining a salary increase? When did we last replace seniority, longevity and survival with something called merit? That is a reshaping of Government.
We were also told that within two years Canada Post will be challenged to pay its way. That is a staggering thought. However, it is not a staggering thought south of the border where the United States Post Office not only pays its way without subsidy but actually shows a profit.
We were also told in the budget address that other Crown corporations will be sold and that further steps will be taken to get the Government out of the private sector. One of the most significant ways in which we are reshaping Government is by getting Government off the backs of the people. I draw the attention of the House to one way in which that has been done and on which we should focus attention. I refer to the reform of the Registered Retirement Savings Plan regulations. Plan-
February 27, 1986

holders will now gain a freedom of which they should never have been deprived. At last, RRSP holders will be treated as adults who have the right to decide how they will spend their own money. No longer will a person cease to be treated as an adult when he reaches the age of 71 and is required by legislation to collapse his RRSP. He can now have a registered retirement investment fund, to which he had been entitled for many years, but will not have the freedom to withdraw from that fund whatever amount he chooses. His retirement years can be shaped by his own choices. There will be a minimum withdrawal required by legislation, but no maximum imposed. Retirees will now be free again, free to live their own lives by making their own choices and by spending their own money. That is an example of what I mean when I say that our policies are reshaping Government itself.
Fourth, we are renewing the economy. Once again, because of our economic policies, Canada is big league. We have had an economic growth rate equal to that of Japan-twice the growth rate of the United States, greater than the growth rate of all the major countries of western Europe. That's big league, especially because the stress has been on generating that growth through the private sector. The expansion has come about for one simple reason, that is, investors again believe in the country. They believe that we have a Government in which they can have confidence. We see this in the way in which month after month the leading economic indicators are up, all of them pointing to the way in which the economy is being renewed. We have heard so much said about the need to help this part of the population and that part of the population. The most important way we can help people is by renewing the economy and giving the people an economy in whose prosperity they can share. We are doing that.
This brings me to the next way in which our policies are benefiting Canadians, namely, restoring employment. Hon. Members are familiar with the macro figure of 580,000 jobs which have been created since our Government took office. We are familiar with the way in which the unemployment rate has fallen to 9.8 per cent, the lowest rate in five years. However, I want to focus the attention of Hon. Members on the way in which the Budget is targeting certain groups of our population and offering them particular assistance in restoring employment. In this regard I refer specifically to young people, women who want to re-enter the labour market and older men who find themselves out of work after years of working for a company or an organization which has suddenly closed down or been taken over. I am thinking of the job strategy programs. I am thinking of the program for older worker adjustment. Each of these programs offers hope and assurance to people who wondered if their futures were not behind them. We are not treating people as statistics. We are treating them as people with feelings and aspirations, people who have a right to dignity and a right to believe that they have years ahead in which they can provide for themselves, live independently and have the dignity of daily work. We believe in that. We are offering it and succeeding in it, as the statistics indicate.
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
As well, our economic policies have aimed at reforming the tax system. The Budget continues the reform measures which were heralded in the 1984 Economic Statement, continued in the Budget of 1985, and which have now been taken a step further in the Budget of 1986. I refer to the reduction of tax avoidance policies, so many of them added by the previous Government. There is the introduction of the minimum tax, a new tax introduced into the fiscal system of the country. There is the removal of several corporate and personal tax breaks which did not contribute to the fairness of the taxation system. I would say that I looked upon these particular reforms as only a first step toward what I believe this country profoundly needs, and needs critically. It needs a more fundamental re-examination and restructuring of the income tax system. The problem with trying particular reforms of the income tax system, worthy and necessary as the effort is in this interim period, is that the structure of the income tax system itself is wrong. No particular changes to it will get at the basic need, which is to start over again with a healthy tax structure which will provide adequate revenues for Government services, equitable distribution of the tax burden and a tax method which will not work against the incentives to expand our production as a people.
I speak here not on behalf of the Government or of my Party but I express only the opinion of a private Member of the House. I hope that the time is not distant when we could have appointed a task force which could address itself particularly and wholly to a fundamental examination and reform of the Income Tax Act, reform that will aim at removing the dominance and monopoly of personal income tax as the main source of financial supply for the Government. I believe that will not only be a measure of social justice but equally it will contribute to the expansion of our productivity as a country.
In those ways, I draw to the attention of the House and the public that this Budget is to be judged in terms of economic policies which, since the fall of 1984, have achieved this objectives which the Government set for itself during the election. We were elected to reduce the deficit, and we are doing it.	We	were	elected to restrain expenditures, and	we	aredoing it.	We	were	elected to reshape Government, and	we	aredoing it.	We	were	elected to renew the economy, and	we	aredoing it.	We	were	elected to restore employment, and	we	are
doing it. We were elected to reform the tax system, and we are doing it. These are the reasons for which we can look forward to the future with the confidence we were denied in the years 1981, 1982, 1983 and 1984 until the election.
The historian Arnold Toynbee once analysed the history of mankind by pointing out that great civilizations have resulted from a combination of challenge on the one hand and response on the other. The people of Canada were faced with a challenge in 1984. They responded by electing a Government able to make a response equal to the fiscal challenge, which has been described in words no more accurate and eloquent than those of the Premier of Ontario, the Hon. David Peterson, who has said that the federal Government inherited a mess. That

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Stackhouse
was the challenge and the Canadian people and the Government addressed themselves to it.
Once to every man and nation comes the moment to decide. In 1984, the people in Canada had that moment and they decided. The success of these economic policies has shown the wisdom of that decision for we are now able to face the challenge and combine it with what is now the assurance of opportunity.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to congratulate my colleague on his excellent address. I would like to give an example of how Government policies could work. In 1972, when the Right Hon. Member for Vancouver Quadra (Mr. Turner) was the Minister of Finance, there were 544,000 people out of work. When he left office, 732,000 Canadians were unemployed. We can see that his record as a Minister of Finance was an absolute disgrace. Since the election, under our Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson), 580,000 new jobs have been created including 129,000 in January. We have turned this record around.
I would like to discuss a disgraceful statement that was made by the President of the Federation of Labour in Alberta. He has been telling the people of Alberta to stay on welfare or UIC and not to take any jobs. In Canada today, there are more than ever job openings and opportunities right across the country, except for a few pockets. There are "help wanted" signs all over the place. Newspapers carry special supplements for "help wanted" ads.
This gentleman to which I refer, Mr. Werlin, has said that no one should take a $4-an-hour job in Alberta. However, the business people have said that many of those jobs are full-time and would pay a junior trainee with no advanced education about $6 per hour or $950 per month. I do not think it is so bad for someone to start with. In fact that people are starting out by making $4, $6 or $8 an hour does not mean they are going to stay at that wage the rest of their lives. If they are ambitious, they will advance.
I would ask my hon. friend what he thinks should be done about the statements of this labour leader. I have passed this information on to the Forget Commission. I want the commission to examine this information to find out why there are so many job openings and yet we still have a high unemployment rate.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF THE MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I think there are two aspects to the question which my hon. friend raises. The first is the possibility some suggest-and in reporting this I do not concur necessarily with the opinion expressed-that the entitlements through unemployment insurances and other Government programs are too great to encourage people to take jobs that are paying a minimum rate. The other possibility is that there are many, many people in society who need to be able to move, not necessarily from one place to another, though that may be part of the answer, but move from one skill to another, from one occupation to another.
If I may quote the economist John Kenneth Galbraith, he has said that historically, mobility has been the solution to
poverty. We are seeing this today, not simply in geographic terms or moving from a high unemployment area to a low unemployment area, but in more sociological and economic terms, with the need to move from skills and occupations that are no longer in demand to those that are in a new demand. That has been the thrust of this Government to a very large degree, particularly in the recently introduced Canadian Jobs Strategy Program and the other programs for older workers to which I had referred.
I have profound confidence that through retraining, educational opportunities and other means, we are going to give people a chance to move from a set of circumstances in which there may be no viable future to another set in which there is promise. They are facing a challenge and this Government is giving them an opportunity.
