subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I just want to begin my discussion this afternoon by referring to one point which was made by the Hon. Member for Scarborough West (Mr. Stackhouse). He feels that budget time provides the people of Canada with the opportunity to judge the performance of their Government. I remind him that not only is judgment being made on a daily basis about the conduct of the Government, but the judgment of the people of Canada is given once every four years or five years at the end of the Government's mandate.
I personally find it galling that the Hon. Member indicated that he was in favour of tax reform. He said that it would
remove the yoke of Government from the backs of individual Canadians and allow private enterprise to fly free again. He stood in his place and defended the Budget. I hope he stays for some cross-examination, but in the meantime I point out to him the document which was tabled yesterday entitled The Fiscal Plan. Page 100 of the document indicates that in 1984, 9 per cent of the Gross National Product was taken up in direct taxes from individuals and that 2.8 per cent was taken up from corporations. I hope the Hon. Member will answer me in about 18 minutes with regard to how he could defend the Government's Budget which increases the percentage of the Gross National Product taken directly from persons under taxation from 9 per cent in 1984 to 10.5 per cent in 1987. In the same period of time, the corporate sector of the economy will be paying even less in taxes. Perhaps he could answer my concern about that. I would be delighted to debate the issue of fairness with him.
The point I want to make today is that the Government will be judged not only on the basis of this Budget but on the basis of the previous one. There is a tendency on the part of Hon. Members opposite to demand that we focus only on the immediate Budget before us. However, I submit that the two Budgets-the Budget of May 23, 1985 and the one of February 26, 1986-are interlinked. A great deal of thought has been put into that interlinkage. The Hon. Member from Prince Edward Island clearly indicated that. I suspect that the two Budgets are the beginning of a plan in which there will be another phase of sales tax increases over the next three years to four years and in which there will be the introduction of a value-added tax to the income tax system. I suspect that some of the social programs introduced in the Budget will be the forerunners of programs which will supposedly protect the poor in society from some of the regressive nature of the tax proposals in the Budget. The fairness issue will be one of the ways in which the Canadian public judges the Government. It is also going to be judged in the way it has handled the regions. On both of those counts the Government will fail.
First, let me talk about the issue of fairness. On May 23, the Opposition indicated to you, Mr. Speaker, our concern about the fiscal intent of the May 23 Budget. We indicated that for the first time in Canadian history, by direct Government taxation, fiscal policy, there will be a widening of the gap between the rich and the poor in our society. Nothing has made us change our minds. What is astounding is that after the debate on the fiscal implications on middle and low-income Canadians that began on May 24, 1985 and ended with the budgetary votes in December, one would have thought the Government had learned its lesson as a result of the debate that took place then.
In addition to the effects of the Budget of May 23, 1985, the gap between rich and poor will widen and be compounded and aggravated by the Budget put forward yesterday. On pages 99 and 100 of The Fiscal Plan the Government will increase taxes this year. The percentage increase on persons from 1984-85 to 1985-86 will be an astounding 17 per cent.
February 27, 1986

That 17 per cent increase in one year is being done in the same year that corporation taxes will be increased by a measly 2 per cent. Yet the Hon. Member for Scarborough West has the gall to tell me he is in favour of a restructuring of the income tax system. He should be in favour of a restructuring of the income tax system, and it should be a restructuring that would allow the Canadian middle class to have less of the burden of taxation than exists today. From the time the Government took office, there has been a consistent fiscal and social policy to widen the gap between the haves and the have-nots.
Let me put this into perspective so the Member for Scarborough West can understand the point I am making. In 1986, a family earning $100,000 a year paid $35,236 in tax. Under the budget proposals tabled yesterday and combined with the Budget of 1985, that family earning $100,000 will pay $34,450 in tax by the year 1988. That family's tax load will decrease by $1,000 over the next three years. However, a family earning $20,000 a year will find its tax bill increased from $1,388 to $1,409 in the same period of time. I question the perverse social logic that would lead a Government to bring in budget legislation that will widen the gap between the haves and the have-nots, between the rich and the poor in our society.
Let us look at the fairness of the taxation changes introduced yesterday. There will be a further increase of 1 percent in the federal sales tax. You have heard it said, Mr. Speaker- it has not been argued in Question Period in questions put to the Finance Minister-that every 1 per cent increase in the federal sales tax results in a further $1 billion being taken out of the economy.
Since September 17, 1984, when the Conservative Government took office, there have been three successive 1 per cent increases in federal sales tax. Three billion dollars has been taken out of the hands of consumers as a result of the federal sales tax changes.
I mentioned earlier that the Government would prefer us to view this Budget in isolation. There is good reason for that, but First I will give the Government credit in the area of social programs. The Government introduced a refundable sales tax credit in this Budget that will give $50 per adult and $25 per child for those with incomes below $15,000.

speechtext: Less than $1 a day.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Can you imagine, Mr. Speaker, that the Conservative Government's definition of a median family income is $15,000 a year? In other words, a family with four children earning $18,100 in 1986 will not get one penny of relief from the federal sales tax. That is the 1 per cent federal sales tax that has been introduced in this Budget. The Government would like us to forget about the sale tax increases in the May 23, 1985 Budget and in the November Economic Statement of 1984.
Let us look at the effect of the Budget in 1985 and 1986 on a family of four with one wage earner earning $20,000 a year. As a result of those two Budgets, that family's income tax will go up by $225 and the wage earner will pay an additional $300
The Budget-Mr. Frith
in sales tax. The Government's social policy is wrong. It has widened the gap between the poor and the rich. It is wrong to expect 4 million Canadian families, who live below the poverty line with $20,000 a year in family income, to share in the burden of deficit reduction, especially at a time in which we are introducing budgetary measures that will lessen the corporate sector's share.
That, Mr. Speaker, is what the Canadian people will judge three or four years from now when we have the next federal election. I am sure Canadians will speak loudly.
In 1950, federal personal income tax amounted to 23.4 per cent of federal tax revenue and, incredibly, corporate income tax at that time was 28.7 per cent. Over the intervening 25 to 30 years, the share of federal tax revenue derived from corporate income tax has decreased to an estimated 17.2 per cent. As I have indicated, by purpose and by budgetary design the amount of dollars expected from the corporate sector over the next three or four years will be further reduced to its lowest point in history as a percentage of the Gross National Product. That is the kind of social Fiscal policy the Conservative Government believes in.
Let us look at some reactions to the Budget of last evening. I am told that the business community was mixed in its judgment on this Budget, but there were several business organizations that were laudatory about the Government's Budget. No wonder, Mr. Speaker. If I were in the private sector in business and found the Government bringing in a Budget that would decrease my tax rates, I would be rather complimentary about the Budget as well.
Who speaks for middle class Canadians and who speaks for the poor, who are being ravaged as a direct result of the Fiscal policy of the Government? It is not the individual back-benchers of the Conservative Party. I have yet to see Ministers on the front bench defend the social policy being instituted by the Minister of Finance.
What other kind of reaction should we judge this Budget by? In the last 24 hours the business community, the money markets, have reacted in a very negative way. As of one hour ago, the Canadian dollar has fallen to 70.65 cents U.S. Yesterday, 24 hours ago, when the Minister of Finance just began his speech on the Budget, the dollar stood at 71.68 cents U.S. The dollar has fallen a full percentage point in the space of 24 hours. That is a shocking indictment and should be of some cause for worry for the Government front benches. The money markets are reacting very rapidly.
On the issue of the way in which the Government is handling its commitments to the regions, not only have we witnessed the Conservative Government, which over two successive Budgets has ravaged the middle and low-income Canadians, but we have witnessed its abandonment of its commitments to the regions of the country. Let me be specific: Atlantic Canada, in terms of the unemployment rate and in terms of the number of dollars being allocated under the Department of Regional and Industrial Expansion; northern Ontario, northern Quebec, Sudbury and parts of western Canada. These regions have not been part of the economic

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Frith
recovery, and the Government has abandoned them. That is the way in which Canadians will judge the Government. Governments are judged on their commitments. In this case I do not take anything away from the Conservative Party. I take nothing away from the fact that we have had an economic recovery in the last 18 months. That recovery has been worldwide, but I will not get into that kind of philosophical argument. I will give the Government credit where it is due. The unemployment rate is down. It is still unacceptably high, but it is down.
However, I appeal to the Government not to abandon the regions of the country which expect the central Government to give them a share of the economic pie of the country. That is what is wrong. The Government has asked that the economic recovery take place only by use of the private sector. It has indicated that there is no role for the Government to play in the economic recovery in terms of public sector involvement. That is wrong.
The International Nickel Company or Falconbridge cannot be expected to be the full engine of growth for economic recovery. MacMillan Bloedel cannot be the sole engine of recovery for the forestry sector in British Columbia. The private sector cannot do all the economic recovery work in Atlantic Canada. The national Government must play a moderating role to ensure that Atlantic Canadians and people from Sudbury have a piece of the economic pie. You cannot simply hive them off and tell them to find a job somewhere in Toronto. Is a 43-year old miner who finds himself unemployed with a young family and a high school education going to be retrained in high tech to find employment in the metropolis of Toronto? The answer is no, and you are wrong if you expect the private sector to play that role.
Every time direct economic programs which abandon commitment to the regions are brought in it facilitates the urbanization of population and abandons the principles that the country was built on 118 years ago. Those are facts which should be borne in mind when discussing the Government's Budget of last evening.
There is another area in which the Government is wrong. It takes great pride in saying that the budget deficit is now below $30 billion. Well, whoopee, Mr. Speaker. Since the Government took office on September 17, 1984, the federal deficit has increased by 23 per cent. Can that be blamed completely on the previous Liberal Government? The answer is no. The Government inherited a budget deficit of $32 billion and it increased it. Now the Government expects Canadians to applaud its efforts to get the deficit below $30 billion.
How was the reduction achieved? Was it achieved through expenditure cuts? The Government is trying to convince the Canadian public that it has done a masterful job on reducing expenditures. Since the Conservatives took office on September 17, 1984, expenditurs have gone up by $7.2 billion. The Government has achieved a projected budgetary deficit in 1986 of below $30 billion by foisting the largest tax increase
on middle-income Canadians in Canadian history. That is the bottom line.
The Government is asking middle-income Canadians, who last year paid $38 billion in personal income taxes, to increase that by $16 billion in one year. These are the figures used by the Finance Minister. At the same time as the Government is asking middle-income Canadians to suffer such a massive tax increase, it is letting corporations get away with paying less and less tax. To me, that is the problem with the Government's Budget. The Government is going to fail in the key area where Canadians will judge the fairness of this Budget because it has placed the whole burden of deficit reduction on the backs of middle and low-income Canadians. It is letting the private sector, free enterprise, and the corporate sector get away scot-free.
Every social policy reform group in the country indicated to the Minister of Finance in December what they felt was wrong with the last Budget and what they felt the next Budget should do to help the poor and middle-income Canadians. They asked for tax relief for low-income Canadians. In this Budget there are tax increases for everyone who has a family income above $18,000 a year. So much for listening to the Canadian public. They indicated that they wanted a tax system which would give personal income tax less of a role and give the corporate sector its fair share of the tax burden. We got the complete opposite in the fiscal policy of the Government. There will be more taxes on middle and low-income Canadians and less taxes on the corporate sector. That is the net effect of the Government's policy.
The social policy reform groups asked the Government to review its decision with regard to the $500,000 lifetime capital gains tax exemption. There is no suggestion in the Budget of even reviewing that. This is the same Government that said it could not find enough money to shield fully low and middle-income Canadians from the devastation of a federal sales tax which everyone in the House agrees is regressive. The level at which low-income Canadians are going to be protected is set at $15,000 a year. The Government cannot find any money from them, but it can afford to give $500,000 worth of capital gains tax free. That is going to be the indictment of the Government that has failed to live up to its commitment of fairness to the Canadian public who will judge it in three years.

speechtext: Mr. Speaker, it was interesting to hear the Member of Sudbury (Mr. Frith) remind us that in 1950 corporate and personal income taxes brought approximately equal amounts to the Canadian Treasury. I remind the Hon. Member that for 30 of the 36 years since 1950, Liberal Governments were in office and gave tremendous tax concessions to the corporations.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Hear, hear!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I mentioned earlier that a Government is judged on its fairness, on how it treats the less advantaged, the poor, and the elderly in society. The Member conveniently used the figures from 1950 to 1984. I take responsibility because I was a member of the Government of the day and, for a very short period of time, a member of the Cabinet. The answer to that is simple. During the intervening 30 years, Canada had the fastest growing population in the western industrialized countries. We had a tremendous job of ensuring that the young people, the less advantaged, and those coming into the workforce, had an equal opportunity to share in the economic pie. As a result of the tremendous pressure on the system the Government was forced to give away certain concessions to corporations in order for them to have accel-lerated capital depreciations so that equipment and machinery could be brought on and job placements for the young could be made. Not once in those 30 years was there a deliberate social or tax policy to widen the gap between the rich and the poor. The Liberal Party always stood for the poor and the oppressed and every one of the social and fiscal policies introduced during those 30 years went towards making sure the gap narrowed between the rich and the poor in our society. That is what is diametrically wrong with this Budget brought down by the Conservatives. It is the first time in living memory that a Government, by deliberate taxation policy, is going to widen the gap between rich and poor. I will stand by the Liberal record any day of the week.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I am not not a great tax specialist or an expert in taxation and I am relying on simple common sense, but in Charlevoix, common sense tells us that you are rich when you do not have any debt, and I believe that the best way to reduce the gap between the rich and the poor in Canada would be to pay our debts. I did say our debts because their debts have effectively become ours, and we have received a mandate to pay their debts, which are now our debts, to bring about a better distribution of our collective wealth among all Canadians. On the other hand, my learned colleague the tax expert said that a 1 per cent increase of the sales tax would take away $1 billion from the Canadian economy. I would like to ask him this: How much has it cost us
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
to have a debt of $200 billion, which is what he left us, and a deficit of $30 billion, which is what we have this year after bringing down to $33.8 billion what, under his Government, was a deficit of $38 billion? How much does this take away from the Canadian economy? Is this not much more painful than the tax increases which we have had to impose? Naturally, the Opposition must criticize, and I think that the Hon. Member does it quite well, but criticizing is not simply saying anything you like. I believe that we have to pay our debts. The Hon. Member also spoke about outlying regions. I represent such a region myself. Do you think that the Government likes having to take $30 billion from the pockets of Canadians? Do you think that we are inhuman? Very often, the Opposition considers that the world is divided into the wealthy, who are insensitive and cruel, and the poor, who work with their hands to pay for the bare necessities of life. Do you think that we are too insensitive to understand the development needs of our regions? I ask this question with the common sense of the people of Charleboix. In the near future, will being wealthy not mean being able to pay our debts, or rather your debts?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, the answer to that question is this: Why did you, the Government, decide to reduce the deficit on the backs of middle income Canadians and poor families? Why did you choose to do this? You had a choice in the Budget and you decided to reduce the deficit on the backs of poor and middle income families, but not on the backs of small businesses or big corporations. You attack only the poor. You will therefore have a problem in explaining your choice to your constituents next week-end.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Well put!

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, it is certainly a privilege for me to enter into the first full day of debate and to be able to express the views from the point of view of a British Columbia Member on the Government side. I would like to use my time today to talk a little bit about the B.C. perspective and some of the tremendous opportunities which this Budget provides for us in British Columbia. I would like to start first by looking at it within the context of what we have heard from the Canadian public and how we have listened and how we have responded.
I find this Budget indicates a Government that, first of all, is firm but is also fair. It shows also a Government that is consistent, but a Government that cares. Those are themes which are indicative of the kind of Progressive Conservative Government that we have in this House. As I went through my riding over the past six months and talked to groups of all kinds from low-cost housing, the business community and the native Indian community, one issue that came up consistently was, "What are you going to do about this deficit that you have inherited?" Most people recognize that it was not this

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
Government's fault, that it was the accumulation of years and years of wanton spending, of not considering the real needs of Canadians and their desire to have a Government that was concise and had a streamlined operation.
Because of the situation we were in they were not quite sure what we could do about it. They were not sure if we were prepared to do anything. People would say, "Are you really going to tackle the deficit? Can you do it without hurting people?" They were saying, "You have got to do it". People were speaking from two points of view. First, people from the business community were saying that the impact of the present load of debt that this country is carrying is having an adverse impact in terms of the international investment community. You will not be able to attract those dollars unless you show that you are a Government that is determined to turn the ship around.
I was hearing it from ordinary Canadians who were saying, "What is this debt going to mean to my children or my grandchildren? If it carries on the way it is at astronomical rates, my kids are not going to have any future. They are not going to be able to pay for old age pensions and I am probably not going to have any kind of retirement."
I am so pleased today to be able to tell my constituents and all Canadians that they have a Government that has guts, that is determined to make those changes and is turning the ship around. It is not easy, but with our performance to date and the Budget we put forward, substantial progress has been made.
Let me just draw your attention to some of the facts. We know that this year we had projected a budget deficit of $33.8 billion. A lot of people said, "Ah, you're not going to be able to meet that target. A number of things have happened, it is going to be higher than that". The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has said, and it was not easy, that with a lot of hard work, and it was not easy, we are going to be able to achieve that objective. We are going to be able to say, "Canadians, you can believe our word. What we say is what we do". That is a very important and strong signal to Canadians.
We have also said in this Budgete for the first time that in the coming year we will reduce that deficit to $29.8 billion on the old accounting system, $29.5 billion on the new accounting system and $23.5 billion on national accounts. It depends which way you want to look at it. No matter how you look at it, that is good news, that is a substantial decrease.
Then you have to look at the forecast, because this Budget should not be viewed in isolation, it is taken together with the November, 1984 Economic Statement, the Budget of last year, today's Budget, and the projections we have put forward, and what we see are really happy news. We see a decrease in that debt down to $22 billion by 1990-91. In terms of Gross National Product, the deficit will fall from what it was last year, 7.7 per cent in 1984-85, down to 3.7 per cent in 1990-91. That means this nation will be $100 billion less in debt than it would have been had the Government not taken the measures it did in the past 18 months. I think it is a remarkable and
extraordinary process which no previous Government could ever have achieved.
The Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) said that as well as looking at the debt, we should look at what our financial requirements are, because that is a very important indicator which is looked at very closely by the international community. The news here is even better. Because of the expenditure controls we have put in place and because of the increased revenues from new taxation measures, our financial requirements will fall from $30 billion in 1984-85 to a projected $11 billion in 1990-91. In terms of Gross National Product, that means a fall of from 7.1 per cent this past year to 1.7 per cent in 1990-91. In five years, following on our course of action, we will only have to borrow $11 billion or 1.7 per cent of the GNP. Just think of how that is going to free up opportunities.
I say, therefore, that this Budget is the first step in terms of trying to attain fiscal stability that we have seen in our country for over 20 years. Of course, it also puts to bed all those nay sayers, those doomers and gloomers, who said yesterday: "Oh, geez. The Budget is not going to create any jobs. We are going to lose all those jobs". Some Hon. Members said that last year, but we know now that it is not true. In the past 18 months there have been 580,000 more jobs created, while we have reduced the Budget and curtailed Government expenditures. I am pleased that 51,000 of those jobs are in my own Province of British Columbia.
How have we been able to achieve some of these tremendous objectives? As the Minister of Finance said yesterday, we have started by getting our own House in order. It started right here in Ottawa. We are all prepared to give up $1,000 this year and that is only fair. But we have done so much more. I find that many people have the perception that there is tremendous fat and waste in Government. I think particularly of British Columbia. That province is so far away, but suddenly there are all those billions and billions of dollars just done away with. People might think that there would not be any impact anywhere, but after one has been around here for a while, one realizes that that is not quite the case. Every program has a group which is affected positively by it. If we are going to do away with programs, we have to be quite sure we know what we are doing away with, and we have to do it carefully and humanely or we may institute more pain and grief. So our approach has been one of sound fiscal management.
The Minister of Finance has announced a decrease of
15,000	jobs in the Public Service by the end of the decade. He is eliminating programs which no longer serve a useful public policy purpose. I think of the PIP grants, the CHIP grants and other programs. We have reduced certain subsidies to VIA where they are no longer required. We are selling off Crown corporations which no longer play a vital role in our public policy. Of course, this year, we are announcing another 2 per cent reduction on all Government expenditures, which will mean $500 million out of the discretionary area and an additional $300 million in the reserves. These efforts will bring
February 27, 1986

Government spending down from 26 per cent of the Gross National Product in 1984-85 to 21 percent by 1990-91.
As we all know, Government spending grew at an annual rate of about 13.4 per cent over the past decade. That is far higher than inflation. Inflation was running at an average of around 8.8 per cent. Government spending was just galloping and consuming more and more of our dollars. This year that has been stopped. We have the motors in reverse. Government spending has been brought down to 3.2 per cent in the coming year. In fact, in the discretionary area, as we have heard already this morning from the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret), it has been basically stopped entirely at a minimal .2 per cent.
What the President of the Treasury Board announced this morning was one of the most exciting prospects. He said we are going to award productivity. There will be new programs to reward people who have new ideas, who work hard and who are productive. In British Columbia, my industries have had a tough time over the last little while, the forest industry and the mining industry. But they did not give up. They became more productive and now have one of the highest rates of productivity. I think we can do that, too. There is a tremendous challenge out there and I know the President of the Treasury Board is going to work hard in that respect.
This Budget also does some other things. It shows that we are targeting our spending more effectively. We are identifying our priorities and we are building on our strengths. We have identified, I believe, some very important areas about which I, in particular, am concerned. The field of research and development, from the perspective of British Columbia, is terribly important. We have all heard, of course, from the funding councils, NSERC, the Medical Science Council and the Social Sciences Humanities Council, which are putting in place five-year programs. There will be $300 million more for those councils.
There has also been a new and extremely innovative idea which will bring together the business sector, these councils and the universities. We will match dollar for dollar up to $700 million over the next five years with a potential increase of $1 billion for those funding councils, and most of it goes directly into the universities. I am not sure that many people realize the tremendous boost that this is going to give to our research and development activities in our universities. In the Budget last year we introduced our new scientific research program where there are certain deductions. I can see that if we put that together with our new program, it will provide tremendous opportunities for companies in my riding which are involved in R and D to work together with the universities. We will have meaningful, exciting research and development opportunities.
I was really pleased to see the focus on the Atlantic Provinces, because they need it. It is a tremendous program. I am pleased as well at the new steps in agriculture. That is not a major factor in my riding, but in the Province of British Columbia it is. The new commodity bonds will certainly be
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
important there. I was pleased as well to see the social programs, targeted programs to help those most in need.

The refundable sales tax credit for lower income families and, of course, the pre-payment of some of the child tax credits are also very positive features. There is the increase in the deduction for disabled people. There are 185,000 disabled people in this country who will certainly benefit from that. We know, and the figures show, that small business creates the largest number of jobs. We also know that women are creating most of the small businesses, or at least a large number.

speechtext:
So we have special measures to help them because we want to encourage them to get established and start those businesses. The reduction in the tax rate, which will come into effect next year, from 15 per cent to 13 per cent; the reduction of the tax rate with respect to manufacturing income from 10 per cent to 8 per cent; and the cancellation of the 12.5 per cent dividend distribution tax, are all measures which are really going to encourage people to start businesses and to expand them. Of course, the improvement of the small business loan, almost doubling at up to $2.5 billion, will make accessible millions of dollars to the small business community. As Hon. Members know, last night John Bulloch said that for small business we are very bullish.
I would now like to tell Hon. Members about some of the reactions to the Budget expressed by people in the West. As reported in The Province of Vancouver, British Columbians are very pleased. The newspaper stated that Ottawa has finally become serious about getting expenditures and revenues in line. The article to which I refer states that the Budget is a credible attempt at financial restraint, but financial restraint with a human face. I think that is an important message. We want to get our house in order. It shows that we want to undertake financial restraint and do things more efficiently but that we will not slash programs that will really hurt people.
I would now like to refer to some of the issues which are of particular excitement to people in the West. I mentioned earlier in the House today one issue about which I am very pleased, that is, the fact that Vancouver has been designated as an international banking centre. We have been looking for a measure of this type for some time. I am glad that my colleagues from Montreal will have the same opportunity in this respect. However, we in Vancouver look to the Pacific, where there are tremendous possibilities in trade. We will be able to develop our whole financial relationship in the Pacific which will give a real leg-up to people in Vancouver in terms of creating excitement and opportunities.
The area of science and technology is a tremendously positive area for British Columbia. In my province we are trying to develop our skills and bring adaptive technology to the province.
There are all sorts of other measures in the Budget about which we are extremely pleased. When one goes through the document quickly one is apt to overlook some of the items which are there. I almost missed the item about the $33 million film program. British Columbia is becoming the home of a burgeoning film industry. This $33 million fund will help Canadian film with cultural content. I particularly liked the caveat which states that film-makers will have to show where the films are actually made and will actually have to identify the place name. That is great because we want Capilano identified in such films. We are certainly open and ready for the film business. It will be profitable for British Columbia.
I would now like to refer to a couple of other areas about which I have received representations. One is with respect to flow-through shares, and the concern that investors in flowthrough shares have a continuing liability. I am pleased to see that the Minister of Finance has made a change with respect to that provision so that investors will no longer have a continuing liability. At the sametime, he closed a loophole, which is only fair. The investors will now only receive a credit up to the amount of money that they have actually invested.
I would now like to talk about the sales tax exemption for tourist literature. That is something for which the tourist industry in British Columbia has been asking for some time. I refer to tourist literature which is prepared and available through chambers of commerce and communities which will now be exempt from sales tax. This a positive step. It is a little thing, but these little things all add up.
I have had a great many letters with respect to Registered Retirement Savings Plans. I am sure that my colleagues have also received many letters from people who are retiring and who want more flexibility with respect to how they deal with their retirement years. The Government has said that it will provide new options for those people in using their RRSPs.
Finally, I would like to deal with the treatment of Canadian dividends and reducing them to one-third. I do not think that will have a dampening effect on the country. However, in responding to some real concerns which I have heard with respect to the minimum tax, Canadian dividends will only be taxed on their actual amount as opposed to the grossed-up amount. In this way there will not be a disincentive to invest in Canadian corporations. That is an important move, and I applaud the Minister of Finance for taking it.
There is so much to talk about. What the whole matter comes down to is that the Budget shows that we are in control. It shows that we are planning and that we are going to stick with our plan. It is a plan that will bring about results. It is working. It shows we are consistent and comprehensive. We have a plan which started back in November and we are following it through with projections. We can show people where it will lead them. I realize that there is some pain involved for everyone, but that is part of what it is all about. In the end we will see a much healthier and dynamic economy.
We have balance because we are reinforcing priorities and strengths. Yet, as I said before, this is restraint with a human face. We are successful, and the record speaks for itself. I hardly need to say more. We have reduced the deficit. We did what we said we would do. We have created jobs. We have a record of success which will carry on for decades to come.
As has been said before, the cumulative effect of all these measures will result in $100 million less indebtedness over the next five years. We have shown leadership. We have listened and acted decisively. That is what the people have asked us to do. We know what has to be done. As the Minister of Finance mentioned yesterday, we have more to do in the future in terms of corporate and personal tax reform.
February 27, 1986

There are a great many challenges that lie ahead of us. We have provided a framework which will enable Canadians to be confident in the Government. It will be a Government to which they can look with confidence. Our children and our grandchildren will inherit a country which is fiscally and humanly well managed.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I congratulate the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins), my colleague from British Columbia. I recognize her enthusiasm and her excellent speaking qualities. I do not think she will mind if, in friendship, I remind her that it is not too surprising that she is so enthusiastic since she comes from a riding which I believe is the wealthiest in Canada. I know there are many wealthy people in her riding who will be pleased with the Budget. Because I know the Hon. Member is sincerely interested in Canadian women and because she shares my concern that they have more equal opportunities, I would like to appeal to her. Even though the Hon. Member comes from a wealthy riding I know she has a sympathy for those who are not as fortunate.
What I would like to ask the Hon. Member has to do with child care. Since she is a parent she will know how important it is for women to get into the workforce. We know that over 50 per cent of workers in the workforce are from two-parent families in which the mother is working. There has also been a great increase in the number of women who are single parents and who are either working and need child care or who would like to work but cannot. The Hon. Member referred to a program which is targeted to women on welfare. It would be a wonderful thing if they could receive training which is related to them in terms of pre-employment training and the like in order to get into the workforce. However, they cannot do that unless there is a relevant, flexible and affordable child care program available to them.
The Hon. Member also knows that we have a child care task force. The need is there. We all know that it is desperate. The statistics show that there has been a change in Canadian families. Is the Hon. Member not disappointed that there was not something in the way of child care in the Budget? This is something that would pay for itself, since these women could get off a life of welfare and into the workforce. What would the Hon. Member like to see in this area?

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to thank my colleague, the Hon. Member for Vancouver East (Ms. Mitchell), for her question. I know her deep commitment to these issues. I did not expect that the Budget would deal with the issue of child care. I say this because of the all-Party committee which has been set up to look into the issue, a committee on which the Hon. Member sits. I know that the committee will be travelling across the country and examining issues. It will be considering how the matter can be dealt with most effectively.
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
It will be working with the provinces since they bear the greatest responsibility for the delivery of services in this area. I know that the committee will come up with proposals and ideas with respect to the most effective way the federal Government can be involved in helping to support families in a variety of ways. I am looking forward to the report of that committee. As the Minister said on Canada A.M. this morning, this is something with which he hopes to deal in the next Budget.
I appreciate this opportunity to respond generally since the Hon. Member raised the issue of the impact of the Budget on women earlier today. Of course, women account for 50 per cent of the population. They are affected by all the different aspects of the Budget. However, there are some important aspects in the Budget for women. I have already mentioned the refund of the child tax credit, which will help many women in their financial circumstances. Of course, there is the refundable sales tax credit for the lower income families, many of which are headed by women. It will be of particular help to them. As the Hon. Member already mentioned, there is a program designed to help those on social assistance find employment. Again, many of those on social assistance may be single mothers who want to get back into the workforce.
In my own riding, I visited very recently a job re-entry program that was set up under the Canadian Jobs Strategy Program and I met with the women. About half of the women were on social assistance and the other half were interested in going into small businesses and wanted to develop the kinds of skills they had not developed before. I was overhwelmed by the tremendous enthusiasm in that program. The women are learning from each other. It has provided them with a real chance. This Budget will enable more programs like that and will increase emphasis on small business-

With the emphasis on small business, many of these women who are looking for opportunities, who are trying to get loans and are not quite sure of the financial situation, will be encouraged to go into small businesses and create jobs.

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mrs. Collins
I would like to comment on two or three things. First, I must allude to the reference made to the proposal for international banking centres in Vancouver and Montreal. We have heard from previous speakers about reaction across Canada. I would like to cite some comments that were made to my colleague from Scarborough. They had voted Liberal in the last election and they said to my friend: "Congratulations, you have done what no other Government has had the intestinal fortitude to do, you are taking firm, decisive steps to reduce the deficit. You have our vote from now on". That is the type of reaction that is coming from across Canada.
In addition, I am sure my colleague might like to comment further on some of the measures that were taken to which she did not refer. For instance, the expenditure on all Government programs being held at 1984-85 levels means a decrease of 4 per cent. The non-statutory programs are to decline by $500 million in the next year, but no reference was made to that. I have to ask my hon. colleague why this is so.
In closing I point out that the impact of expenditure reductions and continued tight management that this Budget has put forward to Canadians will reduce Canada's debt by $78 billion by the end of the next decade. I wonder if my hon. colleague would care to comment on some of those points.

Mr. Speaker, I am so pleased that my colleague brought those points up. As he knows, there is so much in the Budget that one cannot possibly talk about all of the positive things in it in 20 minutes. Hopefully, he will have the opportunity to do so. I am particularly pleased that he raised the points he did.
Regarding the international banking centre in Vancouver, it was groups from Vancouver that originally proposed the idea, as I understand it. We see Vancouver as being the jewel of the Pacific looking toward Asia which has a tremendous trade potential. We have the desire to get involved in China, Japan and Indonesia and the enormous opportunities that exist there. This would have a cumulative effect and would bring the other small industries that we are trying to develop to British Columbia, industries dealing particularly with what we call the adaptive technology area. There are already some examples of joint ventures with our Asian partners in the health field.
We see this international banking centre as the linchpin, the first step in turning Vancouver into what I would call the financial, trade, and institutional centre of the Pacific. With the experience we will get as we are successful in dealing with the East and as Montreal is successful in dealing with Europe, perhaps Toronto, which is now considered the financial centre of Canada, might have an opportunity to expand its bases as well.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, I would like to comment on yesterday's Budget, first in French and then in English. It seems to me that the Conservatives are making the same mistakes as in the Budget of May 1985. They impose severe tax increases to ordinary Canadian families while reducing the tax burden of corporations, and now of the wealthy. They are simply maintaining a pattern which existed under the Liberal administration. For our part, we often think that there is very little difference between the Conservative Party now in power and the Liberal Party which used to form the Government.
In May 1985, Mr. Speaker, the Government attacked mostly pensioners, children, families and the Public Service. This time, the Government has decided to hit mostly ordinary taxpayers and, once again, the Public Service, which is of concern to my constituents.
If I may remind the House, since everyone is now aware of them, the major tax measures in the Budget-there is a 3 per cent surtax hitting all taxpayers, not only those with income above $40,000 a year. There is a 1 per cent sales tax increase, and this is the third sales tax increase since the Tories came to power.
Before the 1984 election, the Conservatives loudly criticized the tax increases imposed by the Liberal Government. But the minute they came to power, they readily introduced the one per cent increase that had been proposed by Mr. Lalonde when he was Minister of Finance. And then, in May, there was a second one per cent increase, and now we have this third one per cent increase. This means that within a period of 18 months, the Conservatives have increased by one-third the federal sales tax. Mr. Speaker, all those increases are directly affecting the average family. And the average family has not yet had an opportunity to answer back, to respond to the Budget.
I was just listening to the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) who suggested that her constituents were satisfied. She quoted from the Vancouver Province. Today we heard quotes from the president of the stockbrokers, from people in the Stock Exchange, in the banks, and from other businessmen. All the financial communities were very quick to react. They are in a position to react very fast, because of their control, advertising agencies, etc.
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
I remember very well, Mr. Speaker, the last Budget brought down by this Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson). Initially, everything seemed to go very well. But within a few days, pensioners, people over 60 years of age started to react. Their reaction continued until the Minister of Finance was forced by his Prime Minister and the whole of the Government to withdraw those key budgetary measures. So much for bad judgment... for he had hit the average people and pensioners in our country. Now he is hitting the average family.
Mr. Speaker, I can quote figures. In the very First Budget, the November 1984 financial statement, tax increases and other charges imposed by the Conservatives on average families totalled $500 a year on average. Then, in May 1984, came another $500 a year increase. And this time, there is an additional increase of $350 a year. All this adds up to $1,350 per average Canadian family. This means that under a Conservative Government, the deficit is fought on the backs of the average Canadian families.
However, Mr. Speaker, if by any chance we look at the Fiscal Plan tabled yesterday by the Minister of Finance, we find that taxes levied on taxpayers are constantly increasing, while big corporations experience practically no tax increases.
In 1984-85, the last year to which the previous Government's tax policy applied, personal income tax went up to $38 billion. Under the former Liberal Minister of Finance, corporations paid $12 billion in corporate income tax.
Personal income tax is increasing from $38 to $44.7 billion in 1985-86 and up to $49.3 billion in 1986-87, and it will go up again, to $54.8 billion in 1987-88. This means that personal income tax will be increased 44 per cent as a result of the tax measures introduced by the Conservatives during their first eighteen months in power.
Mr. Speaker, compare this with the very slight increase in corporate taxes. These taxes will go up by $1.3 billion during the same period, which means 10 per cent, notwithstanding very strong profit increases during the same period as a result of the economic recovery following the recession we had at the beginning of the eighties.
Mr. Speaker, we see that between 1986-87 and 1987-88, there will be a reduction in corporate income tax and of course in the federal Government's revenues from these companies, while tax increases totalling $5.5 billion are being levied on the individual taxpayer. Mr. Speaker, this is not fair at all!
Last year, we on this side of the House criticized the Budget of the Minister of Finance, especially because the Budget was liable to cause the loss of hundreds of thousands of jobs. We do not know exactly what the impact was of that Budget, since most of the tax measures announced in May last year have yet to more an impact since they were not introduced until the beginning of this year.
So what we have are 1985 measures that have just started to have an effect on the economy. At the same time the Budget is

February 27, 1986
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
introducing new measures, we have had the beginning of a slowdown in economic expansion in the United States since last year, and now there is growing concern, since we have had four years of expansion in Canada, that the economy will start to slow down. The business cycle is going to hurt the Government's expectations that the unemployment rate is going to drop.
We have a Budget in which the Government's priority is not to create jobs but above all to satisfy the business community on Wall Street, in London, Paris and Bay Street and St. James.
Mr. Speaker, in the last few weeks we had a Gallup poll done for the New Democratic Party to find out what Canadians thought about tax reform. Ninety per cent of those surveyed answered that they really wanted tax reform because they wanted to see a fair tax system. And they believed that the existing system was not equitable. Unfortunately, there is no indication in yesterday's Budget of any changes that will make the system more equitable.
Mr. Speaker, I would simply like to recall some of the recommendations made to the Minister of Finance by our finance critic, the Hon. Member for Kamloops-Shuswap (Mr. Riis), as well as by myself and other Members on our Tax Probe 1986. Mr. Speaker, we recommended the adoption of an annual Budget of tax expenditures which would show annual costs, tax rebates and the nature of tax rulings. This has been ignored.
We recommended the establishment of profitability tests with respect to specific tax measures. We said: The public has the right to know if our major tax expenditures are effective, just as it has the right to know the impact of our direct expenditures. This has been ignored.
Mr. Speaker, we recommended the elimination of some of the existing tax measures, for instance the lifetime $500,000 capital gains tax exemption which costs at least $600 million a year. We advocated doing away with the tax exemption on interest costs related to mergers and take-overs since it will cost in excess of $200 million this year. Those two proposals have been ignored.
We proposed that the recent increases in RRSPs which cost $40 million be eliminated or reduced. This proposal has been ignored. We proposed the elimination of abuses with respect to corporate transfer provisions which will cost more than $1.1 billion. A few timid steps have been taken, but nothing more. We proposed doing away with the current dividend tax credit which now costs about $1,016 billion a year. Mr. Speaker, it has been reduced by one-third, but two-thirds of this benefit still remain. We suggested that the provisions governing the minimum income tax be strengthened. Manuals are currently being published teaching people how to avoid paying the minimum income tax. A better legislation would bring in at least an additional $100 million.
Mr. Speaker, we suggested that the personal income tax system should be made more progressive. The simple re-establishment of the maximum income tax rates in force before 1982 would result in more fairness and in $1.7 billion in additional tax revenues.
Mr. Speaker, we suggested also to simplify our tax system to make easier to understand.
And we suggested to abolish the tax on gas for farming purposes.
Unfortunately, almost all our suggestions have been ignored by the Minister of Finance, although these suggestions which I have just described would have resulted in between $3.2 billion and $4 billion in savings each year.
This would have contributed to a reduction of the deficit which is a priority of the Minister of Finance and his Government, while giving the Government more spending flexibility, doing away with some required savings and giving it the capability to invest to create jobs in all the regions which need them so much. I am referring especially to Quebec, Mr. Speaker. We still have in Quebec a truly regional problem. Even outside the Gaspe area, we come across unemployment levels which exceed 16, 17 or 18 per cent. In the Temis-camingue area, or in the Lac-Saint-Jean area, as well as in some communities of the Eastern Townships, there are extremely high unemployment levels; yet, there is absolutely nothing in the Budget to meet the needs of the people living in these areas.
On the other hand, as the Hon. Member for Capilano (Mrs. Collins) has just remarked, the Government has just cut its spending in regional and economic development by $14 million, nearly $15 million in 1984-85 and up to $9 million in 1987-88. Apparently, the Government is not overconcerned about the unemployment situation, as we can see from the cuts in the Canadian job strategy where the credits allocated went down from $900 million per year to $800 million per year.
I want to speak a bit about the impact more particularly in terms of people in my riding and Ottawa because of the Budget which the Government has brought down. As I said in French, the Budget is unjust and it puts the burden of deficit cutting on the backs of ordinary Canadian families in my riding and across the country. It does nothing particularly to bring down the rate of unemployment from levels which continue to be unacceptable in Ottawa and across the country. It cuts back sharply in terms of regional development funds and it does nothing to restore the fairness in the tax system, which nine out of ten Canadians have told us in the Gallup Poll they are looking for.
I find it totally unacceptable that the Government is tolerating a situation in 1987-88 where personal tax contributions by ordinary Canadians will go up by $5.5 billion over the preced-
February 27, 1986

ing year and yet in that year corporate tax receipts will actually come down. The Government says it is simplifying and reforming the corporate tax system. The Government forgot that one portion of that tax reform, which is essential and should not be overlooked, is that a fairer revenue from the corporate tax sector should be collected. We should be taking steps now to recover some of those tax revenues from corporations, which revenues have been handed away on a platter, first by the Liberals and now by the Conservatives, over the course of the last eight or ten years.
People in my riding are telling me that they want to see measures to create jobs in this riding, not to destroy them. People in my riding and in the National Capital Region as a whole are extremely uneasy over the most recent announcements that have taken place in the Budget for a further $500 million in cuts in departmental spending, at least a third of which will be felt in Ottawa because that is where the bulk of the Public Service is concentrated. People in my area are concerned over the fact that train services between Ottawa and Toronto and Ottawa and Montreal are now threatened with being cut back or eliminated within a year or two.
They are concerned about training funds decreasing when many people, particularly women, who are coming back into the labour force are still looking for that kind of assistance from Government. In today's economic times with high unemployment, they do not find employers reaching out to provide that kind of training on the job which they might have been able to get a few years ago when unemployment was at more acceptable levels. People in my riding are saying that even if our unemployment rate has come down a bit, what about relatives in New Brunswick where the rate is 14 per cent? What about friends in Newfoundland where the rate is 20 per cent and what about friends in the Province of Quebec where the unemployment rate is 13 per cent? What about my relatives in inland British Columbia from where 1 originally came where unemployment is running at 16 per cent or 17 per cent? Do we not as a country have some responsibility to those parts of Canada as well ? I think we do, Mr. Speaker. I cannot see how we can have a budgetary policy which is essentially directed at Etobicoke, Capilano, Westmount, Rosedale and a few other prosperous areas-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Scarborough, fine-and at a few areas of the country where the financial leader has been telling the Government to cut the deficit and damn the consequences in terms of ordinary Canadians, but that is what we are getting.
In terms of my own riding, the impact of further cuts on top of the 15,000 job cuts already announced in the Public Service is extremely disquieting. 1 fear the cuts are now so severe that Public Service managers will have no choice but to make further job cuts on top of the 15,000 they have been ordered to make. That means more people not just being shuffled around from one job to another, but being thrown out on the street. In my community of Ottawa, it will not be an easy place for people seeking to find employment over the next few years.
The Budget-Mr. Cassidy
Public Service freezes are likely to be the order of the day, not just for a few months but almost continuously. Contract employment is down. Companies that contract with the federal Government will find that the $500 million in cuts will hit them because departments will cut back on spending on those kinds of dicretionary contracts.
The Government is working in cuckoo land if it believes it can make $500 million in cuts and not touch services to the public or not touch the Public Service. I fear that 10,000 more jobs may go. I challenge the President of the Treasury Board (Mr. de Cotret) to deny that and to assure this house that not a single further Public Service job will be cut as a consequence of those $500 million worth of cuts being imposed next year. 1 do not think he can do it.
My numbers would indicate that over the next four years there will be a 5 per cent staff cut. We know about that. Pay rates in the Public Service will go up by 13 per cent of 14 per cent. That has already been agreed to according to the pattern of bargaining over the course of the next few days. That leaves a 9 per cent gap. That gap will not be met by cutting out a few pencils and plane tickets and that kind of thing. You cannot at the same time save Public Service jobs and ensure there is no cut in services to Canadian while still make that degree of cut. You cannot have it that way, Mr. Speaker. I will be watching very carefully, but I am very concerned over what is happening in that area.
The numbers the Government has brought forward indicate quite clearly that the Government could have guaranteed jobs security at the same time it reduced the Public Service by attrition. Seven hundred jobs which the Government says will be lost this year amount to three-tenths of a per cent of the Public Service. If the Government can reach in and find $500 million worth of cuts by means of what it is doing with the cuts announced yesterday, it could find the extra $20 million or $30 million needed to pay for the salaries of three-tenths of a per cent of the Public Service.
If the Government had been prepared and able to negotiate job security with the Public Service and guarantee that no one would be unwillingly deprived of a job, then it would have been able to seek co-operation from the Public Service in terms of getting more effective and efficient management of it. No one who works in Government is opposed to that. People understand the need to make any organizataion work effectively and efficiently. I, as a representative of many people working in the Public Service, support the goal of getting an efficient and effective Public Service of which people who work professionally can be proud.
When you are threatened with cuts, not knowing whether your job is the next on the line, and when the reverse order of merit system is applied so arbitrarily that you cannot be sure that your job will not be chosen regardless of how you have done in the past, the incentive to co-operate disappears entirely. If you co-operate, you might help someone else's merit rating to go up while yours falls, relatively speaking, and you

get dumped. If you train someone new on the job, they may keep the job when cuts have to be made-

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Thank you, Mr. Speaker, for this opportunity to address the Government on its unfair, unjust, and inequitable Budget.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext: Mr. Speaker, I know that my friend and colleague is very knowledgeable about the Public Service, about jobs, and particularly about some of the proposed cuts. I am, of course, concerned about all cuts, but I am particularly concerned about the disproportionate impact that there will be on women workers within the Public Service through Government policies and also through budget cuts. 1 was at a women's conference sponsored by the Public Service Alliance of B.C. and the Yukon last week. People there were very concerned, anxious, and intimidated. Of course, women in clerical and service jobs within the Public Service were the most worried. They were also concerned about contracting out. Women with children will not have the protections they need. Privatization is forcing women into voluntary jobs which do not have adequate wages or protections. They are also concerned about deregulation, which is pushing women into part-time jobs. What comment does my colleague have on this from his review of the Budget and Government policies generally? I would specifically like to ask him about cuts that I noticed in the Budget Papers in the Department of National Health and Welfare. Over the next four years $4.82 billion will be cut from that Department. I believe this will have a very serious impact on women.

subsubtopic: FINANCIAL STATEMENT OF MINISTER OF FINANCE
speechtext:
Earlier today when the Estimates were made available and we had a chance to question officials on them, we asked that very question. We asked whether there is any concern within the Government to ensure that, if lay-offs eventually do occur, although I hope they can all be avoided, women will not suffer. Women tend to occupy jobs as clerks and secretaries, and other jobs which may be seen as being easier to cut by Government mandarins than jobs with more professional or technical qualifications. I had expected the Government to have thought that through, but it has not.
In the recent cuts in the Department of Fisheries and Oceans, an above-average number of women were chopped. I think the Government should make a commitment during the budget debate that if cuts have to take place, no higher proportion of women will be cut than the proportion they form of the Public Service of Canada. That is the very least we could get, Mr. Speaker. In fact, I think it should be the other way around because women have been discriminated against in getting decent jobs within the Government. Perhaps some affirmative action in terms of the de-hiring process might take place as well.
I share my hon. friend's concern about the cuts in the Department of Health and Welfare. We do not know exactly what they mean. However, we know that over time the Government is making greater and greater cuts in the area of health and welfare. Many women who have kids, low incomes, or require training, stand to be badly affected.

speechtext:
Mr. Speaker, the more I listen to socialist Members, the more I understand why Canadians do not take them more seriously. First, the Hon. Member for Ottawa Centre (Mr. Cassidy) began by saying that the Minister of Finance (Mr. Wilson) has imposed a surtax of 3 per cent to all income when we know quite well that the surtax does not apply to all income, but only to taxable income, that is to the amount on which individuals or businesses will have to pay taxes. If that is not misleading the public, Mr. Speaker, it certainly shows a deep ignorance of the facts.
Obviously, Mr. Speaker, the words "tax" and "profit" are always bad for the socialists. I am aware of no one in Canada who wants to pay more taxes than is needed. However, if our friends opposite, the socialists, had not been the crutch of the Liberal Party for 20 years, the Canadian people would not be saddled today with an accumulated debt of over $200 billion. Ordinary Canadians, people in the Ottawa Centre constituency, would not see 80 cents on each tax dollar go to pay the interests on this debt. It is obvious, and I have just had another proof of it, that you are only interested in trying to save your jobs. You sound like a broken record when you speak about the interests of ordinary Canadians. You have been saying the same thing for years. Canadians have been listening to you for years. Moreover, ordinary Canadians have not believed you for years.
Fiscal reform. A while ago he referred to the fiscal reform which is nowhere in this Budget and which was nowhere in the previous one, the "fair imposition" Budget as he called it. I do not know, perhaps this is the Government which introduced a minimum income tax for all individuals. Generally, when we speak of "minimum" for everyone, this implies both the rich and the not so rich. Fiscal reform, with a $500,000 capital gain deduction? They always talk about what it costs, never about what it yields. The RRSPs and what they cost, and so forth.
Mr. Speaker, small and medium businesses ... when he referred to the RRSPs, when he referred to capital gains... you know, you referred earlier to the problems in the Province of Quebec, you referred earlier to unemployment problems in areas such as Lac-Saint-Jean, yes, Lac-Saint-Jean.
